card: The Cabinet Room of the White House, with a tape recorder running. Thirteen days, 16 to 28 October · 22 decisions. Strike, blockade, or something else…
intro: You are John F. Kennedy, 45, thirty-fifth president of the United States. You are in your second year in office. Behind you lie the failure at the Bay of Pigs (April 1961), the Vienna summit (June) and the Berlin Wall (August); ahead, three weeks away, are the midterm elections of 6 November. Around you stand your brother Robert, the attorney general; Robert McNamara, secretary of defense; Dean Rusk, secretary of state; McGeorge Bundy, national security adviser; Maxwell Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs; Adlai Stevenson, ambassador to the UN; Llewellyn Thompson, your Soviet expert; Ted Sorensen, your speechwriter; Douglas Dillon, secretary of the treasury; George Ball, under secretary of state; and John McCone, director of the CIA. In the Cabinet Room and the Oval Office a tape recorder you had secretly installed is running, and your advisers do not know they are being recorded. Times are Eastern Daylight Time, Washington; Moscow is seven hours ahead, Havana one hour behind, London five hours ahead.

JFK-00.place: The White House, meeting of the Special Group (Augmented)
JFK-00.title: Twelve Minutes of Flight
JFK-00.event: After the report of 22 August that Soviet military shipments had surged, you set eight tasks on 23 August in National Security Action Memorandum No. 181: a way to get the Jupiter missiles out of Turkey, a study of the alternatives if missiles came into Cuba, and the pros and cons of a pinpoint strike and of invasion. After seeing the photographs of the SAM sites on 31 August, you told Deputy Director Carter to put that information in a box and nail it shut. On 4 September a White House statement said there was no evidence of offensive weapons such as ground-to-ground missiles in Cuba, and drew a line: were it otherwise, the gravest issues would arise. On 11 September TASS replied that the Soviet Union had no need to move its weapons abroad, and on 13 September you told a press conference that if Cuba became an offensive base for the Soviet Union, the United States would do whatever must be done to protect its own security and that of its allies.
JFK-00.scene: Director McCone has asked again for a U-2 flight. On 10 September, in Bundy’s office, Rusk raised the danger of flights the length of Cuba, citing the U-2 that strayed over Sakhalin and the U-2 lost over China. After that the flights were broken into four, around the island’s edges and on short crossings, and as a result there have been no photographs of western Cuba since 29 August. No one knows what the SA-2 surface-to-air missile sites near San Cristóbal are guarding. McCone’s proposal is a single U-2, flown by a SAC pilot, crossing the western end of the island at 74,000 feet in 12 minutes. Low-level photo reconnaissance could be hit by an SA-2, and a hit would be one more incident before the election. Yesterday you told McCone you would like to hold back the Cuban intelligence until after the election, and in the same breath that something drastic would probably have to be done about Cuba.

voices.who: Rusk (secretary of state, to Deputy Director Carter, 10 September)
voices.text: Pat, can’t you give me a break? How am I supposed to negotiate on Berlin with all these incidents?

voices.who: Robert Kennedy (attorney general, to Rusk, at the same meeting)
voices.text: What’s the matter, Dean, no guts?

Mr. President, the SA-2 is a weapon for shooting down aircraft. There is only one reason the Soviets would ring the west of the island with them: they have something inside to hide. Let us fly just once.

choices.text: Along with the single U-2 flight, send in low-level reconnaissance planes the same day to photograph inside the SA-2 sites
choices.why: To end the doubt, take the whole risk at once
choices.after: Weather put off the low-level flights twice, and on the morning of 14 October Major Heyser’s U-2 crossed the island first, from south to north. 928 frames in six minutes. On the evening of the 15th the National Photographic Interpretation Center found three medium-range ballistic missile sites near San Cristóbal.

choices.text: Approve only a single crossing by a U-2 with a SAC pilot, and put off low-level reconnaissance until you see the results
choices.why: A compromise: answer the biggest question without losing a pilot
choices.after: The weather meant five days of waiting. On the morning of Sunday, 14 October, Major Heyser’s U-2 crossed the island from south to north. 928 frames in six minutes. At 8:30 on the evening of the 15th the National Photographic Interpretation Center found three medium-range ballistic missile sites near San Cristóbal, and Deputy Director Carter telephoned Bundy.

choices.text: Keep the limits of 10 September. Avoid a U-2 coming down before the election, and make do with flights around the edges and agents’ reports
choices.why: Fear that a single incident three weeks before the election could swallow everything
choices.after: McCone came back three days later, and on 10 October Senator Keating told the Senate there were at least six medium-range missile launch sites in Cuba. In the end you approved the flight, and on 14 October Major Heyser’s U-2 crossed the island. On the evening of the 15th the readout showed three missile sites.

note.text: Because of the flight limits of 10 September, there were no U-2 photographs of western Cuba from 29 August to 14 October. At the NSC meeting of 20 October, Deputy Director Cline reported that gap without softening it. Senator Keating’s remarks of 10 October come up again at the first meeting on 16 October.
note.src: FRUS X d421; FRUS XI d11, d12, d18, d34

map.caption: On the morning of 14 October, U-2 Mission 3101 crossed western Cuba from south to north in about six minutes, photographing the area around San Cristóbal.

JFK-01.place: The President’s bedroom, family quarters, the White House
JFK-01.title: A Deadly Secret
JFK-01.clock: Two days until the meeting with Foreign Minister Gromyko

telegram.from: Lundahl, director, National Photographic Interpretation Center (NPIC)
telegram.cc: Bundy, national security adviser (by telephone, 8:30 p.m., 15 October)
telegram.subject: Readout of U-2 Mission 3101, 14 October
telegram.text: Three MRBM sites under construction near San Cristóbal, Pinar del Río Province. / Eight large missile transporters and four launchers in field positions identified. / Probably Soviet SS-4, range approx. 1,020 nautical miles. / Readout of 15 October flights in progress.

JFK-01.event: When Deputy Director Carter telephoned on Monday night, Bundy did not wake you. As he later wrote in a memo, it was a deadly secret and had to remain secret until you could handle it. Calling people in at night would let the secret out, and you were tired, back only the day before from campaigning in New York.
JFK-01.scene: Tuesday morning. You are reading the papers in your dressing gown when Bundy comes in and tells you what the photographs show. The morning papers carry Senator Keating’s remarks about missiles in Cuba, and you had taken him for a liar. Today’s schedule: a meeting with the astronaut Schirra, and preparations for the Connecticut campaign trip. Break the schedule and the reporters will notice. You tell Bundy to have people together by 11:45 and call out the names. Rusk, McNamara, Taylor, Carter in place of McCone, Dillon, Bundy, Sorensen, Ball, Johnson, and your brother Bobby. The question comes up on the spot: can fifteen people keep a secret? Gromyko comes to the White House on Thursday.

voices.who: Bundy (national security adviser, memo of 4 March 1963)
voices.text: It was a deadly secret, and it had to remain secret until you could handle it.

Jack, on 4 September we said there were no offensive weapons, and Dobrynin assured me there were no long-range missiles. Gromyko comes on Thursday. We have to decide what we’re going to do before then.

choices.text: Leave the public schedule as it is and gather just fifteen people in the Cabinet Room at 11:45, in strict secrecy. Let the reporters see no change at all
choices.why: If the secret leaks before a decision, the options vanish
choices.after: You received Schirra and posed for photographs. At 11:50 Lundahl set up his photo boards in the Cabinet Room, and the tape recorder under the table began to turn.

choices.text: Clear the whole schedule and call in the leaders of both parties in Congress this morning to see it too. National consensus comes before secrecy
choices.why: Not wanting to carry the decision alone
choices.after: By afternoon the canceled engagements had become reporters’ questions, and that evening one of the leaders said the word Cuba to a reporter. The 11:50 meeting opened under that pressure.

choices.text: Before the meeting, send Khrushchev a secret letter telling him you know about the missiles, and wait for his answer
choices.why: Open a quiet way back while he still believes you don’t know
choices.after: The letter dragged on for a day as it passed through Bohlen’s and Thompson’s hands, and meanwhile the 11:50 meeting went ahead. No one in the room was in favor of sending a letter first.

note.text: The 14 October flight was flown by Major Heyser of the Air Force, and the two flights of 15 October by SAC pilots. The report format of the readout recasts the content of a FRUS editorial note; no original document has been published.
note.src: FRUS XI d16

pressure.title: News in a Dressing Gown
pressure.text: The night before, you had come back tired from campaigning in New York, and Bundy, judging that calling people in that night would leak the secret, waited until morning. The morning papers carried Senator Keating’s remarks about missile bases in Cuba, and you had long regarded him as a liar. On 31 August, after seeing the SAM photographs, you said to put them in a box and nail it shut. On 10 October, when McCone showed you photographs of Il-28 crates, you said to sit on the intelligence until after the election, yet also that something drastic would have to be done about Cuba. On 10 September, after U-2 incidents over Sakhalin and China, Rusk had the Cuba flights cut back, so the flights across the island stopped; the gap ran from 29 August to 14 October. The midterm elections are three weeks off, and if you break the public schedule the reporters will be the first to notice.
pressure.src: FRUS XI d16; FRUS X d395, d421; FRUS XI d12

JFK-02.time: 11:50 a.m. (6:50 p.m. in Moscow, 10:50 a.m. in Havana)
JFK-02.title: The Fifth Option
JFK-02.clock: About two weeks until the missiles are thought to be operational

map.caption: San Cristóbal is about 1,020 nautical miles from Washington, almost exactly the 1,020-nautical-mile range the United States estimated for the SS-4 (R-12).

JFK-02.scene: Lundahl points to the photographs and explains. Long transporters, tents, mounds of earth that look like launchers. You say that looking at the photographs you couldn’t tell they were missiles, and Lundahl answers that his interpreters have been studying Soviet sites for years. Rusk speaks first. A quick strike, or a political course: inform the OAS and the allies and send Castro a secret message. McNamara says that any air strike must come before the sites are operational, and would take several hundred sorties, against the airfields and nuclear storage as well. Taylor wants to take them out without warning. You ask how many missiles there are in Turkey, and someone answers, about fifteen. The vice president says that of the two he would take them out, and your brother brings up a fifth option. Invasion.

voices.text: I do think we have to set in motion a chain of events that will eliminate this base. I don’t think we can sit still.
If we are to conduct an air strike against these installations, or against any part of Cuba, we must agree now that we will schedule it prior to the time these missile sites become operational.
And then we take them out without any warning.
We have the fifth one, really, which is the invasion.
Both are painful alternatives, but of the two, I’d take them out.

choices.text: Have a strike on the missile sites prepared, but put off the decision. Fly the U-2s to the maximum, keep the secret, and meet again at 6:30 this evening
choices.why: The rule: no irreversible decision at the first meeting
choices.after: You said you were certainly going to do number one: you were going to take out those missiles. What form number one would take was left for the evening. On the way out of the room, no one said the word Cuba in the corridor.

choices.text: Follow Taylor: have a full air strike, including the airfields and the SAMs, readied at once, to hit without warning before the sites are operational
choices.why: The few days before the missiles are up are the only chance
choices.after: McNamara handed the Joint Chiefs a target list, and tactical aircraft began to gather at airfields in Florida. The strike was set for dawn three days later. You kept the Gromyko meeting on the calendar.

choices.text: Take Rusk’s political course. Tell the OAS and the allies first, send Castro a secret message, and split the Cubans from the Soviets
choices.why: A strike without warning would throw away America’s moral standing
choices.after: Assistant Secretary Martin began drafting the message to Castro: unless the Soviet missiles were out within 24 hours, the United States would act. At the evening meeting the draft lay on the table.

note.text: The FRUS transcripts of the two meetings of 16 October are the version the Kennedy Library prepared in the 1980s, and where the speaker is uncertain a question mark remains. The man who answered “About fifteen” is marked “McNamara?” in the transcript. There were in fact 15 Jupiters in Turkey.
note.src: FRUS XI d18; JFKL cmc/oct16/doc2

JFK-03.time: 6:30 p.m. (1:30 a.m. on the 17th in Moscow)
JFK-03.title: If We Put Missiles in Turkey
JFK-03.clock: Carter’s estimate: about two weeks to operational, 4–6 hours to reload
JFK-03.scene: Carter reports that the missiles could be operational within two weeks. McNamara lays out three courses: a political course, which would all but rule out military action later; open surveillance, a blockade and an ultimatum; and military action in stages. Taylor brings out the war plan, to take with 250,000 Americans the island against which 1,800 Cubans were sent a year and a half ago. You say that last month you declared the United States would not stand for this, and they did it anyway, so the risk has grown. Then you ask: isn’t it just as if the United States suddenly put a major number of medium-range missiles in Turkey? Someone answers: we did, Mr. President. Ball says going in like Pearl Harbor frightens him badly. Bundy asks you to approve sabotage, mining Cuba’s harbors.

voices.text: We have a war plan ready for you, Mr. President: 250,000 Americans, Army, Marines and Air Force, to take an island we launched 1,800 Cubans against a year and a half ago.
It’s just as if we suddenly began to put a major number of MRBMs in Turkey. Now that’d be goddamn dangerous, I would think. / Well, we did, Mr. President.
I don’t think there is a military problem here. This is a domestic political problem.
This coming in there, a Pearl Harbor, just frightens the hell out of me as to what goes beyond.

choices.text: Follow Martin’s draft: give Castro a 24-hour verbal message to get the Soviet missiles out, and strike if he refuses
choices.why: Give Cuba the last choice, and the responsibility passes to Havana
choices.after: The message was written but never sent. The next morning the advisers in Ball’s conference room concluded that Castro would use the 24 hours to alert Moscow, and you left on your Connecticut campaign trip.

choices.text: Have options one and two prepared in the greatest secrecy. Hold back the Castro message and the mines, and have a report on the consequences written overnight
choices.why: Prepare, but do nothing irreversible yet
choices.after: You said you did not want to lay mines now. The State Department wrote the report overnight, and the next day you left for Connecticut as planned. Your advisers sat in Ball’s conference room from 8:30 in the morning until 11:45 at night.

choices.text: Approve Bundy’s sabotage: mine Cuba’s harbors and cut off Soviet shipping before the air strike
choices.why: First close the road by which more missiles come in
choices.after: Submarines and covert agents were to lay the mines, but word came back that preparations would take ten days. Within those ten days the missiles would be operational. You left for Connecticut the next day.

note.text: The 250,000 Taylor mentioned was the force for the Joint Chiefs’ Operation Plan 316 (invasion); the 1,800 was the strength of the Cuban exile brigade that landed at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961. The May–Zelikow transcript names Bundy as the speaker of “Well, we did,” but the FRUS version leaves a question mark.
note.src: FRUS XI d21; JFKL cmc/oct16/doc3

JFK-04.title: The Slow Track and the Fast Track
JFK-04.clock: Six hours until the Gromyko meeting
JFK-04.event: On 17 October, while you campaigned in Connecticut, your advisers spent the day in Ball’s conference room. Ball said Khrushchev must be given a way out; Bohlen wanted to send a letter first; former Secretary of State Acheson said the talking should stop and military action begin at once. Rusk proposed informing Macmillan, de Gaulle and Adenauer on Tuesday and making a 52-sortie strike on Wednesday; Thompson and Martin spoke for a blockade after a declaration of war. The Joint Chiefs called a surgical strike on the missiles alone an unacceptable risk. The readout of the 15 October flights turned up two more sites, for IRBMs, which outrange the medium-range missiles.
JFK-04.scene: Rusk says his thinking has changed a great deal in the last 24 hours. That, he says, is how two world wars and Korea began. McNamara says an air strike would kill several hundred Russians and the price would be paid in Berlin. Thompson argues for a blockade after a declaration of war; Dillon says there can be no consulting Khrushchev. You ask about getting the missiles out of Turkey. McCone writes it down. If you act, the allies object; if you don’t, the alliance comes apart. Nuclear war, you say, is obviously the final failure.

voices.who: Acheson (former secretary of state, 17 October, as recorded by McCone)
voices.text: We should proceed at once with the necessary military action and should do no talking.
The possibility of nuclear war, which is obviously the final failure.
Mr. President, Khrushchev has said publicly there are no missiles. A blockade gives him time to back down and save face. A strike takes that time away, and he will answer in Berlin.
A strike would kill several hundred Soviet personnel. Khrushchev won’t let that pass. In Berlin or in Turkey, he will collect the price somewhere.

choices.text: Set up two working groups, one to refine a blockade on the slow track, the other to work up a large-scale strike on the fast track. Have each finish its plan, and choose on Saturday
choices.why: Only when both plans are written out in full can you know what the decision will cost
choices.after: Two groups were formed, one for the slow track and one for quick, dynamic action. Whether to show Gromyko the photographs was left undecided. At 5 p.m. the foreign minister’s car drove through the White House gates.

choices.text: Do as Acheson says: no more talk. Order a full strike without warning, and keep the Gromyko meeting on the calendar to deceive the other side
choices.why: The longer the debate runs, the more the advantage of surprise slips away
choices.after: At 5 p.m. Gromyko said Soviet aid was purely defensive, and you watched his face and did not open the drawer with the photographs. After he left, McNamara reported the date of the strike.

choices.text: Play the withdrawal of the Turkish missiles as a card. Before going public, secretly propose to Khrushchev through Dobrynin that the missiles come out of Cuba and Turkey together
choices.why: Giving up obsolete missiles is the cheapest way to end the crisis
choices.after: Bundy and Rusk objected, and Dillon said NATO would be shaken if Turkey heard of it. You had your brother put the word to Dobrynin all the same. The Gromyko meeting took place before the word reached Moscow.

note.text: The “final failure” passage from the meeting of 18 October is an excerpt checked against the summary on the National Security Archive’s audio page, which quotes the May–Zelikow transcript (“which is obviously the final failure”); the full Miller Center transcript could not be opened. The meeting survives in McCone’s record, and there is a recording, Tape 30.2.
note.src: FRUS XI d28; May–Zelikow (excerpt)

JFK-05.title: Gromyko
JFK-05.clock: Two days until the Saturday meeting, when the decision falls due
JFK-05.event: One room, two reports. Reading from a prepared text, Foreign Minister Gromyko said Soviet aid was purely defensive, and that he wished to stress the word defensive. The next day he reports to Moscow that the overall situation is completely satisfactory and that an American military adventure against Cuba is hard to imagine. You have no way of knowing what he reports.
JFK-05.scene: For nearly two hours Gromyko talks about Berlin and Cuba. You have put the photographs in a drawer. Rusk and Thompson sit beside you, and you slowly read him the 4 September statement, the sentence that says the gravest issues would arise if there were offensive weapons. Gromyko’s expression does not change. You tell him the United States has no intention of invading Cuba, and that this is the most dangerous situation since the end of the war. Bring out the photographs and he will stop lying, but Moscow gains time that very night to hide the missiles or to rush them. Leave them in the drawer, and you must sit and smile through the lies. After the meeting your advisers gather in Ball’s conference room, and at 9:15 p.m. back at the White House. Sorensen later wrote that on that night he moved from an air strike to a blockade.

voices.text: Soviet aid to Cuba is for agriculture and for defense. It is in no way offensive. The American uproar over Cuba is hard to understand.
Mr. President, show him the photographs and he cables Moscow tonight. Then they gain three days and we lose surprise. For now it is better to let them believe we don’t know.
He lied to your face for two hours, Jack. You read him the 4 September statement and he didn’t even blink. It doesn’t matter anymore what they believe.

choices.text: Bring the photographs out of the drawer and send Moscow an ultimatum through Gromyko: unless the missiles are removed at once, the United States will act
choices.why: Better to break the other side’s calculations than to sit through lies
choices.after: Gromyko studied the photographs for a long time and said only that he would report to Moscow. That night word came that cipher traffic from the Soviet embassy had tripled, and you spent the night wondering whether the decision had to be moved up from Saturday.

choices.text: Leave the photographs in the drawer. Read him the 4 September statement as it stands, say you have no intention of invading, and let him go on lying
choices.why: Keep both the advantage of surprise and the time to decide
choices.after: Gromyko left looking satisfied, and you told Rusk he had told you barefaced lies. The 9:15 p.m. meeting at the White House ran past midnight. At 9:45 the next morning the Joint Chiefs are due in the Cabinet Room.

choices.text: After saying you have no intention of invading, propose a private channel between Ambassador Dobrynin and your brother to settle the Cuban question quietly
choices.why: Before a public showdown, build a back door
choices.after: Gromyko said he would pass on the proposal but did not ask what was to be settled. There was no telling whether Moscow had understood, and the next morning the Joint Chiefs came into the Cabinet Room.

note.text: Gromyko’s report of 19 October and Khrushchev’s assessment of 22 October are in the Soviet records published in CWIHP Bulletin 5, and the crossing-point text of this scene draws on crossing point ① of the Phase 1 table. The recollections of Sorensen and Robert Kennedy about that night are secondary sources.
note.src: FRUS XI d29; Phase 1 table, crossing point ①

pressure.title: Lied To a Second Time
pressure.text: In Vienna in June 1961 you sat across from Khrushchev for two days, and when you came home the verdict was that he had pushed you around. Because the word miscalculation was mistranslated into Russian at that meeting, three days from now you will strike it from the draft of your letter to Khrushchev. On 4 September your brother had Dobrynin’s assurance that there were no long-range missiles, and you put it straight into the statement. Now Gromyko, in this room, says again and again that Soviet aid is purely defensive, and the photographs are in your drawer. Bring them out, and Moscow gets time that night to hurry, while the allies, still knowing nothing, hear of an ultimatum. Your brother wrote that he was not at all satisfied that night, and Sorensen wrote that he moved that night from an air strike to a blockade.
pressure.src: FRUS XI d29; FRUS XI d38; FRUS XI d53; Phase 1 table, crossing point ①

JFK-06.place: Cabinet Room, the White House, with the Joint Chiefs of Staff
JFK-06.title: Munich
JFK-06.clock: About an hour until you leave to campaign in Chicago
JFK-06.scene: Taylor, LeMay, Anderson, Wheeler and Shoup are at the table. You explain why you put a blockade and political action first. The Soviets could move on Berlin, and if the United States hits Cuba the allies will say America cost them Berlin. LeMay, the Air Force chief of staff, says he sees the blockade and political action leading into war, and that this is almost as bad as the appeasement at Munich. You are, he adds, in a pretty bad fix. You answer him: you’re in it with me. The room laughs for a moment, and the tape recorder keeps turning. After the meeting you must leave for Chicago to campaign, and your advisers will spend the day in Ball’s conference room over Bundy’s turn toward a strike, the support of Acheson, Dillon and McCone for a strike, McNamara’s blockade and your brother’s memory of Pearl Harbor.

voices.text: I see this blockade and political action leading into war. This is almost as bad as the appeasement at Munich. In other words, you’re in a pretty bad fix at the present time.
You’re in with me, personally.

voices.who: Robert Kennedy (attorney general, to Meeker, the State Department legal adviser, who had asked about the legal basis for a blockade)
voices.text: It’s all politics, not law.
Up to now we’ve been picking holes in the blockade plan, which was a lot more fun. Now the roles will be reversed.

choices.text: Accept the Joint Chiefs’ advice and order a full air strike at dawn on Sunday. Don’t cancel the trip; leave as planned to deceive the other side
choices.why: When the military speaks with one voice, overruling it costs more
choices.after: LeMay nodded, and Taylor reported D-Day for Operation Plan 312 as Sunday. You left for Chicago as planned, and the reporters saw a president with a cold.

choices.text: Cancel the trip, stay in Washington and decide today. Plead a cold, but brief the congressional leaders beforehand
choices.why: At the moment of decision the president must not be away
choices.after: The canceled trip was in that evening’s papers, and by Saturday morning Washington was full of the word Cuba. You had the two scenarios a day early, but the secret had leaked a day early too.

choices.text: Tell LeMay he is in it with you, and leave on the trip. Have the two working groups finish their scenarios, and decide after you return to Washington on Sunday
choices.why: Rather than step straight into the frame the military has built, buy one more day
choices.after: You went to Chicago, and by night your advisers had finished the two scenarios, Alexis Johnson’s blockade plan and Bundy’s strike plan. Stevenson sent in a proposal to demilitarize and neutralize Cuba under UN supervision. On Saturday morning your brother telephoned and told you to come back, and you left Chicago pleading a cold.

note.text: LeMay’s “Munich” remark and “pretty bad fix,” and Kennedy’s “You’re in with me,” were checked against Stern’s transcript (Averting the Final Failure, pp. 123, 126, as quoted in the National Security Archive’s 2022 briefing book). Stern’s version reads “In other words, you’re in a pretty bad fix at the present time” / “You’re in with me, personally”; other versions add “Mr. President.” The State Department meeting of 19 October survives in the record kept by Meeker, the legal adviser.
note.src: Stern 2003 pp.123·126; MC (excerpt) Tape 31.2; FRUS XI d31, d32

JFK-07.place: Oval Room, the White House, 505th meeting of the National Security Council
JFK-07.title: Quarantine
JFK-07.clock: 52 hours 30 minutes until the broadcast at 7 p.m. Monday
JFK-07.scene: Cline reports that 16 SS-4s are operational and could be fired within 18 hours. McNamara lays out the blockade course, adding that if it comes to negotiation you must be ready to give up the missiles in Turkey and Italy and even Guantánamo. Bundy presents the air-strike alternative, and Taylor, the Joint Chiefs, Dillon and McCone side with him. Your brother proposes a blockade, a short wait, then an air strike, which would escape the charge of a Pearl Harbor-style sneak attack. McCone wants a 72-hour ultimatum attached to the blockade. When Stevenson suggests offering to withdraw the Turkish missiles and give up Guantánamo, you cut Guantánamo out sharply. Rusk brings up the word quarantine in place of blockade. It is a word that does not sound like an act of war.

voices.text: The blockade course. But once we are in negotiations we must be prepared to give up the missiles in Turkey and Italy and the base at Guantánamo as well. If we can pay that price, the blockade is right.
The air-strike alternative. A blockade removes not a single missile. What is already in will not come out under a blockade. The Joint Chiefs, Secretary Dillon and Director McCone think the same.
A blockade first, then a short wait, then an air strike would avoid the charge of a Pearl Harbor-type sneak attack.
Mr. President, the speech must contain an offer. If we put the Turkish missiles and Guantánamo on the table, the world will see that America wants peace.

choices.text: Follow Stevenson: put the withdrawal of the Turkish missiles and Guantánamo into the speech as an offer to negotiate, and let the blockade follow
choices.why: Whoever makes the first offer wins world opinion
choices.after: The room fell silent, and your brother looked at you from across the table. Rusk and McNamara said Turkey would have to be told first, and you ordered Moscow’s reaction sounded out through Dobrynin.

choices.text: Choose the blockade. Announce a quarantine on the delivery of offensive weapons in a speech on Monday evening, and keep an air strike on the missiles alone ready for Monday or Tuesday
choices.why: Take a first step that can be reversed, and leave the other side a way to back down
choices.after: You said you would go with the blockade. You ordered that the Jupiters in Turkey and Italy be told not to fire even if attacked, and that their warheads be made removable. Low-level reconnaissance was held back. The speech is set for 7 p.m. Monday; the three networks are asked for air time.

choices.text: Choose Bundy’s air-strike alternative. Strike the missile sites alone at dawn on Monday, and declare the blockade afterward
choices.why: A blockade removes not one of the missiles already in Cuba
choices.after: Taylor called in General Sweeney and had Operation Plan 312 set for dawn on Monday. Your brother said the words Pearl Harbor to you once more as he left the room.

note.text: The word “quarantine” came from Roosevelt’s “quarantine speech” of 1937; it was chosen to distinguish the measure from a blockade, which is an act of war in international law. The decision of 20 October included instructing the Jupiters in Turkey and Italy not to fire even if attacked.
note.src: FRUS XI d34, d35

JFK-08.title: Ninety Percent of the Known Missiles
JFK-08.scene: Sunday morning. General Sweeney, commander of Tactical Air Command, spreads out the air-strike plan: about 40 known launchers, about 500 sorties in the first attack. You ask what percentage could be destroyed, and Taylor answers. Ninety percent of the known missiles is the best that can be done. But the known missiles, McNamara adds, are probably about 60 percent of all those on the island. All three hold that the first strike would have to be followed by several more days of strikes, and that air strikes lead in the end to invasion. You ask your brother and McCone what they think of a strike on Monday morning. Your brother says it would be a Pearl Harbor-type attack and urges a blockade, waiting for the right moment. At 12:30 the British ambassador, Ormsby-Gore, is coming to lunch. He will be the first person outside the United States government to see the photographs.

voices.text: The best we can offer you is to destroy 90 percent of the known missiles.
It would be a Pearl Harbor type of attack. (…) We should go for a blockade and watch for our opportunity.

After the first strike we would have to go on hitting them for several more days, and missiles would still be left. If the ones left are aimed at Florida, it ends with a landing. The moment you order the air strike, you are ordering the invasion too.

Mr. President, I was for the air strike. But a strike on Monday morning without warning would make the world see America differently. A blockade followed by a short deadline, and then a strike, is better.

choices.text: Order a no-warning air strike on Monday morning. Ninety percent is enough, and the second day’s strike takes care of the remaining 10 percent
choices.why: The military calculation: strike when the numbers are best
choices.after: Sweeney saluted and left, and McNamara sent orders to the airfields in Florida. At lunch you laid out both courses to Ambassador Ormsby-Gore, but he could tell you had already decided.

choices.text: No strike on Monday. Declare the blockade, but keep the strike force ready to go on order all week
choices.why: Give up the advantage of surprise and keep a path that can be reversed
choices.after: You refused the Monday strike. The strike force stayed on alert all week. At lunch you laid out both courses to Ambassador Ormsby-Gore and asked which he favored.

choices.text: Separate the air strike from the invasion instead of chaining them together. Hold the strike, but openly begin assembling the invasion force to show the pressure
choices.why: Visible force moves the other side more than words
choices.after: From that afternoon the press photographed troop trains and landing ships heading for Florida. The secret leaked a day early, and the Monday speech became a confirmation of a story everyone already knew.

note.text: The strike plan General Sweeney reported called for about 500 sorties on the first day, and McNamara gave the same figure on 27 October. The meeting survives in McNamara’s memorandum.
note.src: FRUS XI d36; Supp d346

JFK-09.place: Oval Room, the White House, 506th meeting of the National Security Council
JFK-09.title: The Word Quarantine
JFK-09.event: Over lunch Ambassador Ormsby-Gore backed the blockade, saying that of the two courses, hardly anyone outside the United States would regard an air strike as justified. You replied that you and your colleagues had reached the same conclusion. At 2:30 p.m. the 506th meeting of the NSC takes up the third draft of the speech.
JFK-09.scene: Sorensen’s draft lies on the table. Quarantine instead of blockade, the Soviet Union named as responsible, and the word secretly stressed. Stevenson wants the Security Council called first and a summit proposed. You say you do not want to look as if you are clutching at a summit. Whether to stop every ship, allied ships included, is debated, and Admiral Anderson, the chief of naval operations, speaks of a 24-hour grace period after the quarantine takes effect. Someone recalls that at the Vienna meeting Khrushchev took the word miscalculation in a different sense, and the word comes out of the draft letter to him. You direct Nitze to study the withdrawal of the missiles in Turkey and Italy. The question left is whether to limit the quarantine to offensive weapons or to include oil.

voices.who: Ormsby-Gore (British ambassador, at lunch, in telegram 2636 to London)
voices.text: I said that the first course had a very serious defect. Very few people outside the United States would consider the Cuban provocation serious enough to justify an American air strike. Of the two alternatives, therefore, I told him I was clearly in favor of the second.
The United States must call the Security Council first, to keep the Soviets from calling it first. And if we propose a summit, the world will see that America has left the door open.
Blockade reads as an act of war. Write quarantine and it recalls Roosevelt’s 1937 speech, and it gives the lawyers room to fight. I have put in the word secretly three times.
There should be a grace period of 24 hours after it takes effect. That gives ships at sea time to receive their orders and turn back. After that, any ship that does not stop, we will make stop.

choices.text: Include oil and other petroleum products in the quarantine and squeeze the Cuban economy as well. Missiles alone make too weak a pressure
choices.why: A blockade works only if it hurts
choices.after: McNamara said the first shots at sea would come the moment a tanker was stopped, and Thompson said the Soviets would do the same to fuel shipments into Berlin. Oil went into the draft.

choices.text: Limit the quarantine to offensive weapons, put the OAS ahead of the Security Council, and strike the summit proposal from the draft
choices.why: The first measure must be the narrowest and the most justifiable
choices.after: The summit came out of the draft. Rusk arranged to convene the OAS Council on Tuesday morning, and Stevenson prepared the letter calling the Security Council. That night Acheson left for Paris and the letter to Macmillan for London.

choices.text: Follow Stevenson: propose a summit to Khrushchev at the end of the speech. Put the blockade and the meeting on the table the same day
choices.why: Pressure and the way out must stand together in one sentence
choices.after: Bundy and Rusk objected, and your brother said you would look like a president clutching at a summit two weeks before an election. One sentence stayed in the draft all the same.

note.text: At the Vienna meeting of June 1961, when the word “miscalculate” was rendered into Russian, Khrushchev had taken it in a different sense (minutes of the 506th NSC meeting), and at the end of the 21 October meeting the President, remembering this, had the word removed from the draft letter to Khrushchev. Ormsby-Gore’s report is Washington telegram 2636 in PREM 11/3689 at the British National Archives.
note.src: FRUS XI d37, d38; PREM 11/3689 tel. 2636

JFK-10.time: 3–7 p.m. (1 a.m. on the 23rd in Moscow, 6 p.m. in Havana, midnight in London)
JFK-10.place: Cabinet Room, the White House → Oval Office
JFK-10.title: The Seven O’Clock News

telegram.cc: Secretary of State (read aloud at the meeting)
telegram.subject: Reply to the President’s letter on Cuba
telegram.text: First let me say we shall give you all the support we can in the Security Council / This dilemma of being the first to fire has always troubled Britain, and we have always hoped the Russians would be caught in it / Many of us in Europe have lived so long in close proximity to the enemy’s most destructive nuclear weapons that we have got accustomed to it / If Khrushchev comes to a conference he will try to trade his position in Cuba for his ambitions in Berlin and elsewhere. This we must avoid at all costs

JFK-10.event: At 12:17 a.m. the cable left for London, and at 10 a.m. London time Ambassador Bruce handed Macmillan your letter. In Paris Acheson saw de Gaulle at 5 p.m., and de Gaulle said France would act with the United States. In Bonn Adenauer said the President was entirely right. The 11 a.m. meeting considered whether to put into the speech a proposal to withdraw all nuclear weapons from non-nuclear countries, Turkey, Italy and Cuba among them.
JFK-10.scene: At 3 p.m. Rusk reads out Macmillan’s cable, just arrived. You say it is the best argument for doing nothing at all. Rusk calls it a flaming crisis. At 5 p.m. the congressional leadership comes in. Senator Russell asks why you are waiting, Fulbright says a blockade is the worst choice and an air strike would be better, and Vinson says strike with maximum force. You answer that killing Soviet personnel is more provocative than a confrontation over ships, but the leaders’ faces do not soften. At 6 p.m. Rusk hands Dobrynin the text of the speech and your letter to Khrushchev. The letter says you believe no sane man would, in this nuclear age, deliberately plunge the world into war. At 7 p.m. the cameras of the three networks come into the Oval Office.

voices.who: Russell (chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee)
voices.text: Mr. President, why wait? The missiles are there, and more of them every day. A blockade removes nothing.

voices.who: Fulbright (chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee)
voices.text: A blockade is the worst choice. Confronting Soviet ships at sea aims more directly at the Soviet Union than striking missiles on Cuban soil. An air strike is better.
It is a flaming crisis. Still, as a first reaction from Macmillan this is not bad. Britain will clearly stand with us in the Security Council.

I have not assumed that you or any other sane man would, in this nuclear age, deliberately plunge the world into war which it is crystal clear no country could win and which could only result in catastrophic consequences to the whole world, including the aggressor.

choices.text: Give the leadership what it asks and change the speech. Announce tonight that instead of a blockade an air strike on the missile sites in Cuba is under way
choices.why: If Congress turns its back, even a blockade cannot be carried through
choices.after: Sorensen rewrote the speech in three hours. McNamara moved the strike up to dawn, and you pushed the broadcast back a day. Dobrynin went back to his embassy without a copy of the speech.

choices.text: Give the blockade speech as written: the secret Soviet deployment, the quarantine, the demand that the missiles be removed, and an appeal to Khrushchev to pull the world back from the abyss
choices.why: The decision was made on Saturday; Congress will be brought along behind it
choices.after: At 7 p.m. you began by saying that within the past week unmistakable evidence had been established. It ran 17 minutes. When the broadcast ended, Bundy told you the call to Macmillan was through. In London it is 12:30 a.m. on 23 October.

choices.text: Add the proposal from the 11 a.m. meeting. Put into the speech an offer to withdraw nuclear weapons from all non-nuclear countries, Turkey, Italy and Cuba among them
choices.why: A principle persuades the world better than a finger pointed at Cuba alone
choices.after: Before the speech was over Ambassador Hare in Ankara sent an urgent cable, and Finletter, the ambassador to NATO, reported the council in Paris in an uproar. Moscow heard that one sentence.

note.text: The header 222308Z is the date-time group of the copy the White House forwarded to the State Department (received at State 7:43 p.m., 22 October, CAP 5497-62); the cable itself arrived just before the 3 p.m. NSC meeting and Rusk read it aloud (FRUS XI d41, footnote 1). The text gives the 4 passages the Phase 1 report verified against the original. The opening sentence of the 22 October speech was quoted again that night in the letter calling the Security Council.
note.src: NSA #812 Doc 7; FRUS XI d39, d41, d43, d44; S/PV.1022

pressure.title: Two Hours Before the Broadcast
pressure.text: Macmillan’s cable arrived at 3 p.m. When Rusk read the sentence about Europeans who had lived so long beside the enemy’s nuclear weapons that they had grown used to them, you said it was the best argument for doing nothing at all. At 5 p.m., before the congressional leadership, you became the man who had refused the air strike. Russell asked why you were waiting, Fulbright said a blockade was the worst choice, and Vinson said strike with maximum force. All are elders of your own party, men you will be asking for votes alongside in the election two weeks from now. The day before, LeMay had said a blockade was no different from the appeasement at Munich and that you were in a pretty bad fix, and you had answered that he was in there with you. You must keep the public warning you gave in September and still avoid nuclear war, and the last appeal in the speech asks Khrushchev to pull the world back from the abyss.
pressure.src: FRUS XI d41, d43, d44; NSA #812 Doc 7; Stern 2003 pp.123·126 (cited in the NSA 2022 briefing book)

JFK-11.time: Around 7:30 p.m. (12:30 a.m. on the 23rd in London)
JFK-11.title: The First Night Call
JFK-11.clock: About 38 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (10 a.m. on the 24th)

telegram.subject: Reply to the Prime Minister’s cable 222308Z
telegram.text: I fully recognize the dangers you rightly point out, but we also had to weigh the effect of doing nothing in the face of so clear and deep a Soviet challenge / US naval commanders are instructed to use the minimum of force. But I know of no sure way out of the problem of the first shot / Firmness is now the best basic course

JFK-11.event: Two records survive. The American one is a summary memorandum, the British one a verbatim transcript. In the American memorandum you say you intend to begin an escalation in a way that will head off a Third World War; in the British record you say the United States is acting with restraint because it is conscious that the affair could very quickly become a world war or a nuclear war, and that Berlin could be lost.
JFK-11.scene: Macmillan’s voice is slow and roundabout. What do you mean to do with the blockade, end it by occupying Cuba, or just let it drag on? In his long experience, he says, Britain’s weakness has been in not acting strongly enough at the start. What worries him is that if you are drawn into a conference, all the cards are in the other man’s hands. You say an invasion would take 7 days and that you will not invade before you speak to him again. You explain that oil was left out to avoid a counter-measure in Berlin. Macmillan says you must have had a very hard time, and that he has been through such things himself.

voices.text: What do you mean to do with the blockade? Will you occupy Cuba and finish it, or will you just let it drag on? (…) In my long experience, Britain’s weakness has always been in not acting with sufficient strength at the beginning.
What worries me is that if we are drawn into a conference, all the cards are in his hands. The more cards we have in our hands the better, and I should be very glad to see them in yours.
We are trying to begin an escalation in a way that will head off a Third World War. It may come to that anyway, but we cannot accept what he has done.

choices.text: Take up Macmillan’s worry about a conference: tell Britain first that you mean to sound Khrushchev out on a summit, and let London act as go-between
choices.why: Entrust one path to the alliance’s oldest adviser
choices.after: Macmillan paused, then repeated that a conference is most dangerous when all the cards are on the other side. He said Her Majesty’s Government would go along with you, and prepared to face the House of Commons the next day. That night Moscow decided to turn its ships around.

choices.text: Keep the blockade, and promise that an invasion would take 7 days and will not happen before you speak to him again. Consult Britain on the next step
choices.why: An ally’s trust holds when you tell it the next step in advance
choices.after: Macmillan said to wait and see the reaction, and to keep in constant touch through Ormsby-Gore. At 1 a.m. London time he telephoned Ambassador Bruce to say Her Majesty’s Government would go along. The same night in Moscow the Presidium decided to turn the ships around, but Washington does not yet know.

choices.text: Tell him invasion preparations will be complete within 7 days, and ask Britain to stand with you when the time comes. The blockade is the means of buying those 7 days
choices.why: Telling an ally the ending first is the honest course
choices.after: Macmillan said that if it was to end in occupation, it should be done with sufficient force from the start, but he did not say Britain would stand with you. The next day his foreign secretary told the House of Commons only that the American measures were prudent.

note.text: This call is crossing point ③ in the Phase 1 table and appears in the same wording in Macmillan’s seat. The American summary memorandum and the British verbatim record differ, and the Kennedy Library file carries no time, so Macmillan gives it as 11:30 p.m. London time and the British record as 12:30 a.m.
note.src: FRUS XI d45; PREM 11/3689 (NSA #812 Doc 8, 9); Phase 1 table, crossing point ③

JFK-12.time: 10 a.m.–9:30 p.m. (5 p.m. to 4:30 a.m. on the 24th in Moscow)
JFK-12.place: Cabinet Room, the White House → Oval Office
JFK-12.title: Proclamation 3504
JFK-12.clock: 15 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (10 a.m. on the 24th, 1400 Greenwich)

telegram.from: The President of the United States
telegram.to: The Secretary of Defense and the armed forces of the United States
telegram.cc: Citing the resolution of the OAS Council (afternoon of 23 October)
telegram.at: Signed 7:06 p.m., 23 October 1962; effective 1400 Greenwich, 24 October
telegram.subject: Interdiction of the delivery of offensive weapons to Cuba
telegram.text: The Secretary of Defense shall take such measures as are necessary to interdict the delivery of offensive weapons and associated materiel to Cuba / Prohibited materiel: surface-to-surface missiles, bomber aircraft, bombs, air-to-surface rockets and guided missiles, warheads for any of the above weapons, mechanical or electronic equipment to support or operate the above, and any other items the Secretary of Defense may designate / Any vessel proceeding toward Cuba shall comply with directions to stop and submit to search. A vessel that fails to comply or is found to carry prohibited materiel shall be taken into custody / Force shall be used only in case of failure to comply, and only to the extent necessary

JFK-12.event: At 9 a.m. Rusk addressed the OAS Council, which adopted its resolution at 5 p.m. with one abstention. At 4 p.m. in New York Stevenson gave the opening speech in the Security Council. At 5 p.m. Khrushchev’s letter arrived through the embassy in Moscow: the American measures are a serious threat to peace, and the weapons in Cuba, whatever their kind, are purely defensive. You sent a reply: the affair began when the Soviet government secretly supplied offensive weapons to Cuba, and both sides should show prudence and do nothing to make the situation harder.
JFK-12.scene: At 10 a.m. the first meeting of the Executive Committee opens. What if a U-2 is shot down over Cuba? McNamara wants immediate retaliation against the most likely SAM site, and a proposal is put up to delegate the decision to the secretary of defense when the President is unavailable. Six low-level reconnaissance flights are approved. At the second meeting, at 6 p.m., the proclamation is reviewed, and at 7:06 p.m. you sign it in the Oval Office. Whether to add oil to the prohibited list comes up again. After the signing, alone with your brother, you say: it looks really mean, doesn’t it? But there was no other choice. Your brother answers that there was no choice; otherwise you would have been impeached. At 9:30 p.m. he goes to the Soviet embassy to see Dobrynin.

voices.text: If a U-2 is shot down, we strike the most likely SAM site at once, on the spot. If you are not available, Mr. President, you must delegate the order to me. We cannot wait hours.

voices.who: Robert Kennedy (attorney general, alone with the President in the Oval Office)
voices.text: There was no choice. You would have been impeached. / Well, I think I would have been impeached too.

voices.who: Robert Kennedy → Dobrynin (9:30 p.m., RFK memorandum)
voices.text: I said that I felt this action by Khrushchev and the Russians was hypocritical, misleading and false.
Without oil on the list, Cuba can hold out for months. But the moment we stop a tanker, that ship is a Soviet ship, and that is where the first shots are fired.

choices.text: Write automatic retaliation against the SAM sites into the orders if a U-2 is shot down, and add oil to the prohibited list. Squeeze hard from the first day
choices.why: Rules nailed down in advance are rules the other side does not test
choices.after: Oil went into the proclamation, and the Joint Chiefs received orders to retaliate for any shoot-down. Thompson said fuel shipments into Berlin could be cut off the next day, and your brother went to see Dobrynin all the same.

choices.text: Leave oil out, and delegate retaliation for a shoot-down to the secretary of defense only when the President is unavailable. Send your brother to Dobrynin to convey your meaning
choices.why: The decision on the first shot must stay in human hands
choices.after: At the Soviet embassy your brother told Dobrynin he had come on his own initiative and that the President felt deceived. Dobrynin said he did not know what instructions the ships’ captains had. Moscow had already turned 16 ships around, but that night Washington does not know it.

choices.text: Put off signing the proclamation a day. Sign after the world has seen the OAS resolution and the Security Council debate, to make the legal ground firmer
choices.why: A day of legitimacy is worth more than a week of force
choices.after: The proclamation was signed on the evening of the 24th and put off to take effect on the 25th. In that day several Soviet ships crossed the blockade line into Cuba, and the congressional leaders telephoned the White House with the photographs in their hands.

note.text: The text of Proclamation 3504 is a public document; here the prohibited items and the enforcement provisions are given in summary in formal style. The signature block of the original gives the time as 7:06 p.m., while McCone’s memorandum in FRUS (the record of the 6 p.m. meeting) puts it at 6 p.m., a discrepancy. The list of prohibited items matches the original. The “impeached” exchange was verified from the National Security Archive audio page, which quotes the May–Zelikow transcript (1997) directly; the Miller Center’s original transcript could not be opened.
note.src: FRUS XI d47, d48, d50, d51, d52, d53; May–Zelikow (excerpt); JFKL cmc/oct23/doc4; Proclamation 3504

JFK-13.place: Cabinet Room, the White House, 3rd meeting of the Executive Committee
JFK-13.title: The Quarantine Line
JFK-13.clock: Quarantine line in effect; about 2 hours until the first possible interception

map.caption: The quarantine line ran in an arc 500 nautical miles from Cape Maisí and took effect at 10 a.m. Washington time on 24 October.

JFK-13.event: Yesterday, the 23rd, at 10 a.m. Moscow time (3 a.m. in Washington), the Presidium decided to turn back the ships carrying weapons, but Washington does not know it. In New York Acting Secretary-General U Thant is preparing his first letter, appealing to both sides for 2–3 weeks of restraint, and Khrushchev, in a reply to the British philosopher Russell, has spoken of a summit. SAC has raised its alert one level toward full readiness.
JFK-13.scene: McCone reports. Two Soviet ships, the Gagarin and the Komiles, are approaching the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba), and a submarine has taken position between them. McNamara says that with a submarine beside the ship of greatest interest, an interception means dealing with the submarine first, and that could end in sinking it. The Navy has set a procedure for signaling a submarine to surface with practice depth charges, and the procedure has been communicated to Moscow. You put your hand over your mouth. Then a note is passed to McCone: a report that several Soviet ships have stopped or turned around. It is unconfirmed. If the interception goes ahead as planned, the first boarding comes within the hour.

voices.text: There is a submarine right beside the ship we were watching most closely. To stop that ship we have to deal with the submarine first, and if it does not surface when signaled, we have to attack it. The submarine could be sunk.
Mr. President, a report just in from naval intelligence. Six Soviet ships bound for Cuba appear to have stopped or turned around. Confirmation will take about an hour.
The six ships of greatest interest have turned back. Two others are changing course.

choices.text: Go ahead with the interception. The report of ships turning back is unconfirmed, and if the blockade line is breached on the first day the blockade is finished
choices.why: Slackness on the first day undoes ten days of pressure
choices.after: A destroyer signaled the nearest Soviet ship to heave to. The ship did not slow, and the submarine was beneath it. In the afternoon came confirmation that 6 other ships had turned back, but the confrontation at sea had already begun.

choices.text: Call off the depth-charge signaling procedure against the submarine and hold the interception too. Whatever else, prevent a clash with a Soviet submarine at sea
choices.why: The fear that an accident under the sea becomes a war no one ordered
choices.after: McNamara said it would take time for the Navy to accept the instruction, and Admiral Anderson said that if the submarine was left alone the quarantine line meant nothing. At 3:25 p.m. Bundy telephoned Ball. The 6 ships of greatest interest had turned back.

choices.text: Hold the interception for at least an hour. Track and photograph ships that are turning back, and stop and search only those that keep coming
choices.why: When the other side backs down, do not block its way
choices.after: You ordered that no target be intercepted for an hour. Rostow’s subcommittee proposed dividing the ships: those turning back to be tracked and photographed only, those coming on to be stopped and searched. At 3:25 p.m. Bundy telephoned Ball. The 6 ships of greatest interest had turned back.

note.text: This scene is crossing point ⑤ in the Phase 1 table. The turning back of the Soviet ships had already been decided at 10 a.m. Moscow time on 23 October; Washington confirmed it only on the morning of the 24th. The procedure for signaling a submarine to surface with practice depth charges was reported by McNamara to the Executive Committee on 24 October and communicated to Moscow, but it was never passed on to the submarines. SAC’s move to DEFCON 2 appears in the Executive Committee record of 12 November as “SAC remains at DEFCON 2”; the time of 10 a.m. on the 24th rests on SAC’s official history (Historical Study No. 90), whose text could not be opened.
note.src: FRUS XI d55, d57, d58, d59; Phase 1 table, crossing point ⑤; FRUS XI d170

pressure.title: The Moment Your Hand Covered Your Mouth
pressure.text: Last night, after signing the proclamation, alone with your brother, you said it looked really mean, and he answered that otherwise you would have been impeached. You promised Macmillan that an invasion would take 7 days and would not happen before you spoke to him again. This morning, as McNamara reports a submarine beside the ship of greatest interest, the procedure for signaling a submarine to surface with practice depth charges has been communicated to Moscow but not to the submarines at sea. At the Bay of Pigs you learned that what happens on the water does not move at Washington’s bidding. The Navy says the blockade line must be seen to be enforced, and the report that Soviet ships have stopped is still unconfirmed. Tonight you will tell Ball that the impression the Russians are backing off is not accurate.
pressure.src: FRUS XI d55, d57, d58, d63; FRUS XI d45; May–Zelikow (excerpt, quoted on the NSA audio page)

JFK-14.time: 8:25 p.m. to 1 a.m. on the 25th (3:25–8 a.m. on the 25th in Moscow)
JFK-14.title: A Way Out
JFK-14.clock: About 5 hours until the tanker reaches the quarantine line at 2 a.m.

telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.cc: Translated by the American embassy in Moscow, received 9:24 p.m.
telegram.subject: Reply to the President’s letter of 23 October
telegram.text: You have not declared a quarantine, but issued an ultimatum / The Soviet government cannot instruct the captains of Soviet vessels bound for Cuba to obey the orders of American naval forces / To stop Soviet vessels on the high seas is outright piracy, the folly of degenerate imperialism / The Soviet Union will take the measures it deems necessary in response

JFK-14.event: At 8:25 p.m. Bundy telephones Ball. McNamara thinks it important to intercept one tanker and turn it back, but it cannot be done at night, and whether to do it at dawn rests on the President’s decision. At 9:24 p.m. Khrushchev’s letter comes in: he cannot instruct his captains to obey the US Navy’s orders to stop.
JFK-14.scene: At 10:30 p.m. you telephone Ball. They are obviously not going to stop; Khrushchev is stopping only the ships that must not fall into American hands; and the impression tonight that the Russians are backing off is not accurate. At 11:15 p.m. you call again. A message must go out that gives them a way to halt the shipments without appearing to cave in completely. U Thant could be that way out. Ball telephones Stevenson, who wakes U Thant after midnight and arranges a second appeal: Soviet ships to stay outside the quarantine line, the United States to avoid interceptions. At 12:30 a.m. Bundy reads the draft reply to Khrushchev: the responsibility lies with Soviet deception. At 2 a.m. the tanker reaches the line.

voices.text: They’re obviously not going to stop. He’s only stopping the ships that shouldn’t fall into our hands. (…) There seems to be an impression tonight that the Russians are backing off, and that isn’t accurate.
We have to put out a message in a way that gives them a way out of stopping the shipments without appearing to cave in completely.
If it takes the form of U Thant appealing to both sides, Khrushchev is answering the United Nations, not giving in to the United States. Stevenson is waking the secretary-general now.
The secretary-general wants a 2–3 week standstill: both sides stop and negotiate. If we take that appeal as it stands, the missiles stay where they are for those 2–3 weeks.

choices.text: Accept U Thant’s appeal for a 2–3 week standstill as it stands. Suspend the quarantine, the Soviets suspend their shipments, and negotiate in the meantime
choices.why: Taking the hand the UN holds out wins world opinion
choices.after: Stevenson worked on the wording with U Thant through the night. In the morning Khrushchev replied that he accepted the appeal. The destroyers on the quarantine line stayed where they were, and work on the missile sites in Cuba did not stop.

choices.text: Go ahead and stop the tanker at 2 a.m. If Khrushchev has ordered his captains not to comply, find out at sea how far that order goes
choices.why: A line declared in words must be enforced at least once
choices.after: Ball objected, and Bundy said it was the President’s decision all the same. At 2 a.m. a destroyer signaled the tanker Bucharest to heave to. The tanker did not slow.

choices.text: Hold off stopping the tanker and steer U Thant’s second appeal toward American wording. Reply to Khrushchev that the responsibility lies with the Soviet Union
choices.why: Use the UN to give the other side a way to stop while saving face
choices.after: At 1:45 a.m. the reply was delivered to the Soviet embassy. At 2 a.m. the State Department cabled Stevenson to see U Thant again at 8:30 a.m. and shape the appeal. At 7 a.m. the tanker Bucharest passed through the quarantine line without being boarded.

note.text: Khrushchev’s letter of 24 October was a private letter; the original carries no number in its header, so the field is left blank. The text gives the passages the Phase 1 report verified against the original (ultimatum, inability to instruct the captains, piracy). U Thant’s first appeal went out on 24 October, and his second on 25 October along the lines the United States proposed.

JFK-15.place: Cabinet Room, the White House, 4th and 5th meetings of the Executive Committee → telephone
JFK-15.title: The Bucharest
JFK-15.clock: About a day until the East German passenger ship reaches the quarantine line
JFK-15.event: At 7 a.m. the tanker Bucharest passed through the quarantine line without being boarded, and Havana celebrated its arrival. At 1:15 p.m. U Thant’s reply came in. At 4 p.m. in the Security Council in New York, Stevenson told Ambassador Zorin to answer yes or no whether the Soviet Union had placed medium-range missiles in Cuba, and said he was prepared to wait until hell freezes over. Eight low-level reconnaissance aircraft crossed the island as if rehearsing an air strike.
JFK-15.scene: The 5th meeting, at 5 p.m. Tomorrow the East German passenger ship Völkerfreundschaft reaches the quarantine line with 1,500 passengers aboard. McNamara opposes stopping her; Taylor, Dillon and McCone ask what the blockade means if she is not stopped. Your brother says an air strike to destroy the missiles would be better than stopping Soviet ships on the high seas, and Dillon says the confrontation should take place in Cuba, not on the high seas. Rusk suggests buying up tramp freighters and creating a nuclear-free zone in Latin America; McNamara speaks of night reconnaissance with flares. McCone reports. Some of the strategic missiles are now operational. At 6:30 p.m. you speak to Macmillan. You say you cannot let Khrushchev establish the principle that he decides which ships go through and which do not.

voices.text: It would be better to knock out the missiles by an air strike than to stop Soviet ships on the high seas.
The confrontation should take place in Cuba, not on the high seas.
Some of the strategic missiles are now operational.

voices.who: Stevenson → Zorin (Security Council, New York, 4 p.m.)
voices.text: Do you, Ambassador Zorin, deny that the USSR has placed and is placing medium- and intermediate-range missiles and sites in Cuba? Yes or no? (…) I am prepared to wait for my answer until hell freezes over, if that’s your decision.
We cannot permit him to establish the principle that he decides which ships go through and which do not.

choices.text: Let the passenger ship through, and the tankers too, but give notice that an embargo on jet fuel is the next step. Decide after seeing the outcome of the U Thant talks
choices.why: The blockade cannot prove itself against a ship carrying 1,500 passengers
choices.after: Macmillan called it a very skillful and very cool course, and said it was what you had to do. The next morning the Lebanese-flagged Marucla was boarded and searched. She was under Soviet charter, and carried no weapons.

choices.text: Stop and search the passenger ship. Even with 1,500 aboard, a blockade line is a blockade line, and the Soviets must not be able to hide weapons behind passenger ships
choices.why: Make an exception and the other side sends only exceptions
choices.after: McNamara asked that his dissent be entered in the record. The next morning a destroyer signaled the passenger ship to heave to, and the East German captain, saying he was awaiting instructions from Moscow, did not slow.

choices.text: Approve night reconnaissance with flares and add the oil embargo at once. If there are operational missiles, there is no more time to wait
choices.why: The fear that if you cannot see the night’s work, the missiles will be standing by morning
choices.after: That night flares burst over San Cristóbal, and Cuban anti-aircraft guns fired at American aircraft for the first time. Rusk said the U Thant talks were shaken, and Moscow called the night flights a provocation.

note.text: In this call Macmillan spoke of two stages: first the ships, second the weapons actually in Cuba. The same day in Moscow the Presidium decided to trade the withdrawal of the missiles for a pledge not to invade (crossing point ⑥), and Washington did not know it. The Marucla, boarded and searched on 26 October, was a Lebanese-flagged ship under Soviet charter.

JFK-16.time: 10 a.m.–9 p.m. (5 p.m. to 4 a.m. on the 27th in Moscow; 9 a.m.–8 p.m. in Havana)
JFK-16.place: Cabinet Room, the White House, 6th meeting of the Executive Committee → Oval Office
JFK-16.title: The Knot
JFK-16.clock: 48 hours, the deadline you gave Macmillan

telegram.kind: Letter (cable from the embassy in Moscow, received in 4 parts)
telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.cc: American embassy in Moscow (sent from Moscow 7 p.m., 26 October); received at State 6–9 p.m.
telegram.subject: Reply to the President’s letter of 25 October
telegram.text: From your letter I got the feeling that you have some understanding of the situation and a sense of responsibility. I value this / The weapons in Cuba are defensive, and if assurances were given that Cuba would not be invaded, the necessity for the presence of our military specialists in Cuba would disappear / You and I should not now pull on the ends of the rope in which you have tied the knot of war, because the more the two of us pull, the tighter that knot will be tied / Only lunatics want war

JFK-16.event: In the morning the boarding and search of the Marucla was completed. McCone reported that the CIA was suspending the operations of the 10 teams it had been infiltrating into Cuba by submarine, and you agreed. At 1:30 p.m. Fomin, counselor at the Soviet embassy, invited the ABC correspondent Scali to lunch and asked whether the State Department would be interested in a deal: the missiles removed under UN supervision, in return for an American pledge not to invade. From 6 to 9 p.m. Khrushchev’s long letter came in, in 4 parts. In Havana that same night Castro was at the Soviet embassy writing a letter to Khrushchev. This is crossing point ⑦.
JFK-16.scene: At the morning meeting you said that the only ways to get the Soviet strategic missiles out of Cuba were to invade or to trade. Stevenson is negotiating a 24–48 hour standstill in New York, and McCone is against it. Bundy says that if the talks fail, the choice is between widening the blockade and an air strike. At noon the White House issued a statement that work on the sites is continuing. In the evening Thompson reads Khrushchev’s letter. He judges it to be Khrushchev’s own writing. Dimly, inside it, is a trade: a pledge not to invade for the removal of the missiles. At 7:45 p.m. Scali meets Fomin again and tells him the US government sees possibilities; Fomin says time is very urgent and very short. In a late call Macmillan proposes immobilizing Britain’s Thor missiles for the duration of a conference, and you answer that you will put it into the machinery.

voices.text: The only way to get the Soviet strategic missiles out of Cuba is to invade or to trade.
You and I should not now pull on the ends of the rope in which you have tied the knot of war, because the more the two of us pull, the tighter that knot will be tied.

This was not written by the Foreign Ministry. Khrushchev dictated it himself. It is the writing of a frightened man, and there is a deal in it: say you will not invade Cuba, and he takes the missiles out.

voices.who: Stevenson (ambassador to the UN, by telephone from New York)
voices.text: U Thant wants a standstill of 24 to 48 hours. The Soviets stop the work, we stop the quarantine, and in between the secretary-general mediates. If we accept, the Soviets will accept too.
They will not stop the work during a 48-hour standstill. A standstill we cannot verify by photograph only gives them time to get the missiles up. I am against it.

If we want to help the Russians save face, would it be worth our while to undertake to immobilize our Thor missiles here in England during the conference? / (Kennedy) Let me put that into the machinery and I will be in touch with you.

choices.text: Follow Stevenson into a 24–48 hour standstill. Suspend the quarantine, the Soviets stop the work, and U Thant mediates
choices.why: The moment the door to negotiation opens, open it wider
choices.after: That night Stevenson conveyed acceptance of the standstill to U Thant. Moscow said the next morning that it would accept. McCone told the photo interpreters to watch day and night for whether the work stopped.

choices.text: Follow Bundy and have an air strike prepared for dawn on Monday. The letter is meant to buy time, and operational missiles cannot be left in place any longer
choices.why: The work in the photographs is the truth, not the words in the letter
choices.after: Taylor reported D-day for Operation Plan 312 as Monday morning. Thompson said the letter should still be answered, and you put the reply off to Monday. On Saturday morning Radio Moscow read out a different letter.

choices.text: Send word through the Fomin channel that the United States sees possibilities. Keep the path to negotiation open, but give Macmillan a 48-hour deadline. Write the reply tomorrow
choices.why: Keep the way out open, but push the other side with a deadline
choices.after: That night you told Macmillan that if nothing came of it within 48 hours you would face the question of what to do next. Answering the letter was left for Saturday morning. At 10 a.m. Saturday, Radio Moscow began reading a different letter.

note.text: Khrushchev’s letter of 26 October came in through the embassy in Moscow in 4 parts in the embassy’s translation, and FRUS prints the full text. Macmillan’s Thor proposal is in the Kennedy Library transcript; the FRUS record of the same call mistranscribes the passage as “keep an eye on the exiles in England,” so the two versions differ. No American record of what followed “put that into the machinery” was found in Phase 1.
