JFK-17.time: 10 a.m. (5 p.m. in Moscow, 9 a.m. in Havana)
JFK-17.place: Cabinet Room, the White House, 7th meeting of the Executive Committee → Oval Office
JFK-17.title: A Very Fair Trade
JFK-17.clock: About a day until the tanker Grozny reaches the quarantine line; U-2 reconnaissance flight in progress

telegram.kind: Letter (broadcast publicly by Radio Moscow, delivered officially afterward)
telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.at: Moscow, 5 p.m., 27 October 1962 (10 a.m. in Washington)
telegram.subject: Cuba and Turkey
telegram.text: You are worried about Cuba. You say it is 90 miles from the American coast. But Turkey lies right next to the Soviet Union, and you have placed there the destructive missiles you call offensive / We propose: the Soviet Union removes from Cuba the means you regard as offensive, and the United States removes its corresponding means from Turkey / Persons entrusted by the Security Council verify on the spot that each side carries out its pledge. The Soviet Union will make a solemn pledge in the Security Council to respect the borders and sovereignty of Turkey and not to invade Turkey / The consent of the governments of Cuba and Turkey is required

JFK-17.event: After the meeting opens, along with a report that the tanker Grozny is 600 miles out, a note comes in that Radio Moscow is reading a new letter. It contains Turkey, which yesterday’s letter did not. The same morning Moscow has reconfirmed to its forces in Cuba the ban on using nuclear weapons, and in Havana the letter Castro wrote the night before is on its way to Moscow. You know none of this.
JFK-17.scene: Nitze says the Turks would be appalled at the withdrawal of their missiles, Ball says the State Department cannot even raise the subject with Turkey, and Bundy says you must not be seen to sell out an ally. You say you had tried to get the Jupiters out more than a year ago because they had become useless. If it looks as if you are attacking Cuba in order to keep useless missiles in Turkey, the United States is in a bad position; the United States cannot propose withdrawing the Turkish missiles, but Turkey can. After the meeting, in the Oval Office, you tell Bundy and Sorensen: it is going to look like a very fair trade. Your brother says it must be made clear again and again that Cuba and Turkey are separate matters. At noon the White House issues a statement: the work must stop first.

voices.text: If we appear to be attacking Cuba for the purpose of keeping useless missiles in Turkey, we will be in a bad position. We cannot propose to withdraw the missiles from Turkey, but the Turks could offer to do so.
It’s going to look like a very fair trade.

Mr. President, you cannot settle Cuba while appearing to sell out an ally. Until yesterday Turkey was a country the United States had said it would defend. Answer yesterday’s letter. Treat today’s as if you had not seen it.

The State Department cannot even raise the subject with Turkey. The moment we do, Ankara tells the NATO Council in Paris, and the council says America has sold Europe. Talk of substituting Polaris submarines can come only after that.
We have to make it absolutely clear that Cuba and Turkey are separate. Settle Cuba first, then talk about NATO separately afterward. Let’s have the statement written that way.

choices.text: Answer a public offer publicly. Reply today that the Jupiters in Turkey and the missiles in Cuba should be removed at the same time under UN supervision
choices.why: No nuclear war over 15 useless missiles
choices.after: Bundy left the room, and Rusk began drafting cables to Ankara and Paris. In the afternoon Radio Moscow welcomed the President’s answer. That evening a U-2 over Cuba did not come back.

choices.text: Reject the trade in a public statement and demand first that the work in Cuba stop. Warn Turkey of the danger of the coming week
choices.why: A public trade destroys an ally’s trust at a stroke
choices.after: The noon statement went out. You said Turkey had to be told what danger it would be living in over the coming week. At a 2:30 p.m. meeting at the State Department your brother proposed letting the Grozny through, to avoid a confrontation at sea and buy time for an air strike on Monday or Tuesday. At 4 p.m. you went back to the Cabinet Room.

choices.text: Follow Ball and make no public answer. Send only a private letter, keep the blockade, set no deadline, and wait for the Soviets to tire
choices.why: The cold judgment that whoever hurries loses this game
choices.after: No statement went out, and the letter went privately. Work on the missile sites continued, and every morning the photo interpreters added one more to the count of operational launchers. The election of 6 November drew near.

note.text: “It’s going to look like a very fair trade” was verified only from an excerpt of Miller Center Tape 40. The letter of 27 October was broadcast first by Radio Moscow and reached Washington ahead of its official delivery; the text in this scene gives the Turkey passages of the letter as printed in FRUS. The US government had been studying the withdrawal of the Turkish Jupiters since 1961, and NSAM 181 of 23 August also asked how it might be done.

JFK-18.time: 4–7 p.m. (Moscow 11 p.m.–2 a.m. on the 28th; Havana 3–6 p.m.)
JFK-18.place: Cabinet Room, the White House; ExComm, eighth meeting
JFK-18.title: Black Saturday
JFK-18.clock: About 38 hours until the air strike the Joint Chiefs recommend (dawn Monday)

telegram.kind: Memorandum (recommendation of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, reported orally by the chairman, General Taylor)
telegram.subject: Recommended operations against Cuba
telegram.text: 1. Recommend execution of OPLAN 312 (air strike) early morning Monday 29 October. / 2. Recommend execution of OPLAN 316 (invasion) seven days after the strike. / 3. In view of ground fire against low-level reconnaissance today and one U-2 not returned, recommend attack on the SAM site concerned on 28 October. / 4. Propose call-up of Air Force reserve units and start of requisition of civilian shipping.
telegram.sign: Taylor, Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff

JFK-18.event: At 10:20 a.m. (Havana) a U-2 was hit by a Soviet surface-to-air missile over Banes in eastern Cuba and went down; the pilot, Major Anderson, was killed. The same morning a U-2 out of Alaska strayed into Soviet airspace over the Chukotka Peninsula through a navigation error and got out with Soviet fighters on its tail. In the afternoon, in the Sargasso Sea, American destroyers are dropping practice depth charges on the Soviet submarine B-59. In Havana, the letter Castro wrote last night has reached Moscow. This is crossing point ⑧.
JFK-18.scene: McNamara reports. The daytime reconnaissance flights came under ground fire and one plane has not come back. Rusk raises the Alaska U-2's violation of Soviet airspace. You are said to have muttered that there is always some son of a bitch who doesn't get the word. Two drafts of the reply to Khrushchev are on the table, Stevenson's and the State Department's. You have a sentence put in saying you are willing to discuss NATO matters once the Cuban question is first settled, and you say that if you refuse to discuss a trade and then take military action against Cuba, the United States will be in a difficult position too. Taylor reads the Joint Chiefs' recommendation. Air strike Monday, invasion seven days later. McNamara says that with reconnaissance planes being fired on, a limited strike is no longer possible; it will take 500 sorties, and invasion has become almost inevitable. In the evening the loss of the U-2 and the death of the pilot are confirmed. Taylor recommends attacking the SAM site tomorrow. In the next room your brother and Sorensen are rewriting the reply. It answers only yesterday's letter.

voices.text: Now that our reconnaissance planes are being fired on, a limited air strike against Cuba is no longer possible. (…) Invasion has become almost inevitable.

The Chiefs recommend OPLAN 312 Monday morning and 316 seven days later. And the SAM site that brought down the U-2 today must be hit tomorrow morning. If we do not hit it, tomorrow's reconnaissance plane goes down too.

Mr. President, answer yesterday's letter. Yesterday's letter was written by Khrushchev; today's was written by the Presidium. If he gets a pledge of no invasion, he can say he saved Cuba, and that is something he can step back on.
The reply must state plainly that we are willing to discuss Turkey. The world heard the Soviet proposal today, and a reply that only refuses will read as America choosing war over a deal.

The U-2 from Alaska strayed over Chukotka through a navigation error and came out again. Soviet fighters scrambled. On their side it may be read as reconnaissance before an attack. We have to tell Moscow it was an accident.

choices.text: Follow Taylor's recommendation and strike the SAM site that brought down the U-2 in retaliation tomorrow morning. Keep the rule set on the 23rd
choices.why: Break a rule you set in advance and the next threat will not be believed
choices.after: The order went to Florida. You still had the reply sent. That night your brother met Dobrynin but said nothing of tomorrow morning's attack. At dawn the tactical aircraft flew for eastern Cuba.

choices.text: Accept the Soviet public proposal. Instead of an air strike, agree to simultaneous withdrawal from Turkey and Cuba, and promise NATO a Polaris replacement
choices.why: On the day one pilot has died, a resolve not to choose more deaths
choices.after: When the meeting ended and the vice president asked why not trade, Ball answered that Polaris could replace the missiles. You had that answer put into the public reply. At 8 p.m. the letter left for Moscow.

choices.text: Send a public letter answering only yesterday's letter. Trade removal under UN observation for lifting the quarantine and a pledge against invasion, and send your brother to Dobrynin
choices.why: Of the two letters, answer only the one you can accept
choices.after: You decided to send the reconnaissance planes out again tomorrow without escort and to decide tomorrow whether to return fire. The NATO Council is not convened, only briefed. At 7:15 p.m. your brother telephoned Dobrynin and asked him to come to the Justice Department. At 8:05 p.m. the letter left for Moscow.

note.text: Who gave the order to shoot down the U-2 that day is disputed (Garbuz testified that Grechko decided in Pliyev's absence; Malinovsky's report names no decision-maker). The pilot Major Anderson's name does not appear in the FRUS text and rests on secondary sources. The Joint Chiefs' recommendation is what Taylor reported orally at the meeting, recast here in memorandum form; the original document is not in the public record. "There is always some son of a bitch who doesn't get the word" comes down through Hilsman's memoir To Move a Nation (1967); the page number has not been verified. The pilot's name, Major Rudolf Anderson Jr. (the first recipient of the Air Force Cross), follows Air Force records.

pressure.title: Major Anderson
pressure.text: On the 23rd you approved the rule that if a U-2 went down, the most likely SAM site would be struck at once in retaliation, and you delegated the decision to McNamara for when you were absent. You made that rule, and Taylor is asking to carry it out as written. The same morning a U-2 from Alaska strayed into Soviet airspace, and you are reported to have said there is always some son of a bitch who doesn't get the word. In the morning Moscow put the Turkey trade out in public, and you said that if the United States appeared to attack Cuba over useless missiles in Turkey, it would be in a difficult position. Two months ago, on 23 August, you had already ordered a study of ways to withdraw the Jupiters, and at today's meeting you said you had been trying to get them out for more than a year. McNamara says a limited strike has become impossible and invasion almost inevitable, and in the next room your brother and Sorensen are rewriting the letter. Refuse an air strike on the day a pilot died, and Congress and the military will ask why.

JFK-19.time: 7:15–8:05 p.m. (Moscow 2:15 a.m. on the 28th; Havana 6:15 p.m.)
JFK-19.place: Oval Office, the White House → Justice Department, the attorney general's office
JFK-19.title: Words for Your Brother
JFK-19.clock: 50 minutes until the letter goes out (8:05 p.m.); about 35 hours until the air strike the Joint Chiefs recommend

telegram.cc: Copy delivered to the Soviet Embassy, Washington; released to the press
telegram.subject: The President's letter to Khrushchev
telegram.text: Have read your letter of 26 October with great care and welcome your stated desire to seek a prompt solution. / First thing to be done is for work on offensive missile bases in Cuba to cease and for all weapons systems capable of offensive use to be rendered inoperable under effective UN arrangements. / If that is done at once, the United States would, in return for (a) removal of these weapons systems under UN observation and a halt to their further introduction, (b) remove the quarantine promptly and give assurances against an invasion of Cuba. / Thereafter prepared to discuss broader questions of other armaments and easing of world tensions, the matters raised in your second letter.

JFK-19.event: After the meeting you stay behind in the Oval Office with Rusk, McNamara, Bundy, Thompson, Sorensen and your brother. This is where you settle what your brother will tell Dobrynin. Rusk has prepared one more path. If the trade is refused and the negotiation is blocked to the end, a statement in which U Thant publicly proposes simultaneous withdrawal from Turkey and Cuba is to be left with Cordier, the former under secretary-general. That step was never taken, and Rusk disclosed it only in 1987.
JFK-19.scene: Your brother is to say three things. First, work on the sites is continuing, and today a U-2 was shot down and the pilot killed. Second, a decision must be made within 12 or 24 hours; if they do not remove the bases, the United States will remove them, and if Americans die, Russians will die too. This is not an ultimatum but a statement of fact. Third, Turkey. Khrushchev demanded Turkey in public, and there will be no public trade. But what your brother may say in private remains open. The Jupiters are coming out in any case. Say so, and it becomes a deal; leave it unsaid, and all Khrushchev is left with is a statement of fact. At 7:45 p.m. your brother meets Dobrynin in the attorney general's office at the Justice Department.

voices.text: I said that this was not an ultimatum but a statement of fact. He should understand that if they did not remove those bases, we would remove them. (…) If Americans were killed, Russians would be killed too.

I said there could be no quid pro quo, no deal of that kind. (Struck-through sentence: If some time elapsed—and per your instructions I mentioned four or five months—I said I was sure that these matters could be resolved satisfactorily.)

It was clear to me that President Kennedy would not let the Jupiters in Turkey become an obstacle to the removal of the missile sites in Cuba, because the Jupiters were coming out in any event. He instructed me to telephone the late Andrew Cordier (…) That step was never taken.
Dobrynin has to be told about Turkey. But as a fact, not a deal. The Jupiters come out within a few months, but make them a condition now and nothing happens. Khrushchev will hear that.

choices.text: Put the Turkish withdrawal in a secret letter and hand it to Dobrynin. Nothing public, but Khrushchev gets a document
choices.why: A document moves the other side more than words, and the secret can be kept
choices.after: Your brother handed over the envelope, and Dobrynin took it without reading it. Everyone in the room knew that one day the document could be made public in Moscow. At 8:05 p.m. the public letter went out.

choices.text: Give no private assurance. Deliver only the statement of fact and the demand for an answer by tomorrow, and say only that Turkey is not for trading
choices.why: One secret promise puts every later promise in doubt
choices.after: Dobrynin asked again about Turkey, and your brother answered only that there was no deal. The ambassador spent the night writing his cable. Whether Moscow decides before it reads that cable is something you cannot know.

choices.text: Say Turkey is not a trade, but have your brother pass on, by word of mouth only, the President's private assurance that the Jupiters will go within 4–5 months once the crisis is over
choices.why: Give the other side a reason to step back without paying the price of a public trade
choices.after: Your brother said it, and in the memorandum he gave Rusk on 30 October he wrote the sentence and struck it out. Dobrynin spent the night writing his cable. At 8:05 p.m. the public letter left for Moscow, and at 9 p.m. ExComm met again.

note.text: In Robert Kennedy's memorandum of 30 October the sentence about Turkey and "4–5 months" is struck through, while Dobrynin's cable of the same day (Soviet-side research report) recorded the assurance. The U.S. government did not officially acknowledge this private assurance until the 1980s. The Rusk–Cordier plan became known through Rusk's letter of 1987.
note.src: FRUS XI d95, d96, d99

pressure.title: Words to Leave Only in Your Brother's Mouth
pressure.text: Your brother is the man who, on the night of the 23rd, went to Dobrynin alone without telling you and called the Soviet conduct hypocritical and false. It was he who, on 4 September, received Dobrynin's assurance that there were no missiles. The Jupiters in Turkey are missiles you have been trying to get out for a year, but Nitze said Turkey would hate it and Bundy said it would look like selling out an ally. Rusk has left a statement with Cordier for U Thant to propose simultaneous withdrawal if the trade is blocked to the end; that path was never used. Give it in writing and Khrushchev can publish the document; give it only in words and the U.S. government can later deny them. On 24 April 1963 the last Jupiter in Turkey came down, and the U.S. government did not officially acknowledge this night's private assurance until the 1980s.

JFK-20.place: Cabinet Room, the White House; ExComm, ninth meeting
JFK-20.title: Twenty-four Squadrons
JFK-20.clock: About 10 hours until tomorrow's reconnaissance flights; no telling when Moscow will answer

telegram.to: U.S. Mission to NATO, Paris (Ambassador Finletter)
telegram.cc: Embassies Paris and London (gist of Khrushchev's letter of 26 October)
telegram.subject: Guidance for NATO Council briefing
telegram.text: 1. President wishes NATO briefing to be essentially factual and to reflect determination to hold present course as set out in Saturday noon White House statement, President's letter to Khrushchev, Defense announcement of continued reconnaissance and announcement of Air Force reserve call-up. / 2. Khrushchev letter received night of 26 October may be reported as polemical but as offering hope of settlement within framework of withdrawal of offensive weapons under UN observation. / 3. Make no reference to Jupiters in Turkey. Do not indicate preferred course or enumerate alternatives.

JFK-20.event: General Norstad, the Supreme Allied Commander Europe, has cabled urging that the trade be refused. Ambassador Hare in Ankara has been instructed not to raise the Jupiters first. Personal letters have gone to de Gaulle and Adenauer. That night, in the Sargasso Sea, B-59 surfaced and the searchlight of an American aircraft swept its bridge. You have not yet had that report.
JFK-20.scene: McNamara proposes calling up 24 Air Force reserve squadrons, 14,000 men and 300 transport aircraft, and you approve. It is needed for the invasion plan, and it puts pressure on the Soviets. He also wants to start requisitioning civilian shipping tomorrow. You say that if tomorrow's reconnaissance planes are fired on and you learn the result of U Thant's talks with the Soviet side, you will take out the SAM sites by air strike. The Grozny is to be let through, but the Eastern-bloc ships behind it stopped. You do not approve the draft of a separate letter to Khrushchev about the U-2. What remains is what to tell NATO. Offer a preferred course, lay out the alternatives, or state only the facts. In the evening, before your brother left to meet Dobrynin, McNamara asked him whether he had any doubts, and your brother answered that they were doing the only thing they could do. McNamara said it would be an eye for an eye, and Dillon said that was the job. Someone said to make Bobby mayor of Havana.

voices.text: I propose calling up 24 Air Force reserve squadrons, 14,000 men and 300 transport aircraft. The invasion plan needs it, and it puts pressure on the Russians. Tomorrow we have to start requisitioning civilian shipping, or there will be no ships for an invasion.

voices.who: McNamara ↔ Robert Kennedy (evening, before your brother left to meet Dobrynin)
voices.text: Any doubts, Bobby? / No, none. We're doing the only thing we can do.
It'll be an eye for an eye. / That's the job.
We must give NATO facts only. Show a preference and the Council will try to vote on it; lay out alternatives and Turkey will find its own name among them.

JFK-21.time: 9 a.m.–4:35 p.m. (Moscow 4–11:35 p.m.; Havana 8 a.m.–3:35 p.m.; London 2–9:35 p.m.)
JFK-21.place: Cabinet Room, the White House; ExComm, tenth meeting → Oval Office
JFK-21.title: The Day of the Doves
JFK-21.clock: About 1 hour until the scheduled reconnaissance flights

telegram.kind: Letter (broadcast by Radio Moscow; received on the FBIS ticker from 9 a.m.)
telegram.from: Khrushchev, Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR
telegram.subject: Reply to the President's letter of 27 October
telegram.text: Have received your message of 27 October. Express satisfaction and thank you for the sense of proportion you have displayed and for your realization of the responsibility which now devolves on you for the preservation of the peace of the world. / Both you and the Soviet Union understand that the weapons you describe as offensive are formidable weapons indeed. / In order to eliminate as rapidly as possible the conflict which endangers peace, the Soviet Government has given a new order to dismantle the weapons you describe as offensive, and to crate and return them to the Soviet Union. / The Soviet Union agrees to UN representatives verifying the dismantling of these weapons. Give assurances that the United States will not invade Cuba.

JFK-21.event: Moscow made its decision in the morning at the dacha at Novo-Ogaryovo. Castro's warning of imminent invasion, relayed by Ambassador Alekseev; Malinovsky's report of the U-2 shootdown; Dobrynin's cable. Whether the Presidium decided before or after seeing Dobrynin's cable remains disputed. The 5 p.m. Moscow broadcast is 9 a.m. in Havana and the "2:15" that Macmillan heard in London. In Havana, Castro first heard the letter on the radio; in the Sargasso Sea, B-59 did not hear it. This is crossing point ⑨.
JFK-21.scene: At 9 a.m. the FBIS ticker types out the TASS text. Dismantle, crate, return. By the time the meeting opens at 11:10 everyone has read it. Bundy speaks. Everyone knows who were hawks and who were doves, but today is the day of the doves. McNamara says the Grozny is lying stopped outside the quarantine line, so no decision to stop a ship is needed today. You halt today's reconnaissance flights and have a way sought to switch to UN reconnaissance. You say the Il-28 bombers are to be included among the weapons the United States calls offensive, but not to get hung up on them. Your brother arrives. Dobrynin has notified him of the removal. You telephone Eisenhower, Truman and Hoover. At 4:35 p.m. the reply goes out. That you and I were aware that developments were approaching a point where events could become unmanageable. In the evening Rusk tells Ormsby-Gore there are no secret deals, and that there must be no gloating.

voices.text: Everyone knows who were hawks and who were doves, but today is the day of the doves.
The Grozny is lying stopped outside the quarantine line. No decision to stop a ship is needed today. What about reconnaissance? If today's flight is shot down, everything turns over.
Mr. President, a broadcast is a broadcast. Until photographs confirm the dismantling, nothing is over. The Il-28 bombers are nowhere in that letter. Nor is subversion in Latin America.

I think that you and I, with our heavy responsibilities for the maintenance of peace, were aware that developments were approaching a point where events could have become unmanageable. So I welcome this message and consider it an important contribution to peace.
There are no secret deals. (…) There must be no gloating.
voices.src: FRUS XI d106 (memorandum of conversation, indirect)

choices.text: Set conditions first. Withhold any welcome until inclusion of the Il-28s and UN verification are agreed, and leave the quarantine and reconnaissance in place
choices.why: A promise received in words is no promise until photographs confirm it
choices.after: The reply did not go out until evening, and the word welcome was not in it. Moscow waited a day, and in Havana Castro put out five conditions. In the end the road was the same, ending on 20 November with the withdrawal of the Il-28s and the lifting of the quarantine, but the three weeks in between were rougher.

choices.text: Welcome it at once, with reservations. Leave verification, the Il-28s and an end to subversion in Latin America as later tasks; halt today's reconnaissance and send the reply
choices.why: On the day the other side steps back, do not push him from behind
choices.after: At 4:35 p.m. the reply was released from the White House. In the evening Rusk told Ormsby-Gore there were no secret deals and that there must be no gloating. U Thant left for Havana on 30 October, and the quarantine was suspended for two days.

choices.text: Accept it even without UN verification. Halt reconnaissance at once, pledge non-invasion in a formal document and finish it today
choices.why: Ending it today comes before confirmation
choices.after: The reply went out at noon. McCone put on record that removal could not be confirmed without photographs, and Castro refused UN inspection. In the end the United States had to confirm the dismantling by low-level photography in November, and the non-invasion pledge never became a formal document.

note.text: This scene is crossing point ⑨ of the Phase 1 table. The broadcast time is 5 p.m. Moscow (FRUS footnote), while Macmillan told the House of Commons "2:15"; whether the two agree depends on when British Summer Time ended, and the point remains open. Khrushchev's secret letter of 30 October (seeking to put the Turkey understanding in writing) was, according to the research literature, not accepted by the American side and returned (secondary).

JFK-B1.title: The Eve of D-Day
JFK-B1.clock: About 7 hours until the first wave takes off

telegram.to: CINCLANT, Admiral Dennison; Commander, Tactical Air Command, General Sweeney
telegram.subject: Execution of OPLAN 312
telegram.text: 1. Execute OPLAN 312 at sunrise D-Day. / 2. First-wave targets: MRBM sites San Cristóbal and Sagua la Grande, IRBM site Guanajay. Second-wave targets: SAM sites, airfields, Il-28 concentrations, suspected nuclear storage facilities. / 3. No prior warning. Soviet personnel casualties accepted as unavoidable. / 4. Guantánamo reinforcement complete. OPLAN 316 (invasion) forces maintain D+7 readiness. / 5. SAC on full alert.
telegram.sign: Taylor, Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff

JFK-B1.scene: Hundreds of tactical aircraft have gathered on the airfields of Florida, and Marines have moved into Key West. Sweeney's plan: about 500 sorties on the first day, 90 percent of the known missiles. The known missiles are perhaps 60 percent of all those on the island. Hundreds of Soviet personnel will die, and no one knows where Khrushchev will answer. Berlin, Turkey, or from Cuba with the missiles that remain. The allies have not been told. Sorensen has written the speech to be read after the strike, and your brother no longer says the words Pearl Harbor. Before you lie two kinds of document. The execution order, and a letter you could send Khrushchev on this last night.

voices.text: Mr. President, the pilots have been briefed. You can withdraw the order until dawn. After that you cannot. The first day means nothing unless you also approve the second day's wave.
Jack, you can still turn back. You can still declare the blockade tonight. Once the strike is over, what kind of president you are is settled, and it will not change.

An air strike does not end with the air strike. If the missiles that remain are turned on Florida, we have to land. The 316 forces will be ready at D+7. I will take it that you are ordering that as well.

choices.text: Carry out the dawn strike as ordered. Approve the second day's wave as well, and tell the world in a speech after the strike
choices.why: Throwing away a prepared surprise attack on the last night is the greater weakness
choices.after: At dawn the first wave went in over San Cristóbal. At 9 a.m. the photo interpreters reported two-thirds of the launchers destroyed, and no one could count the Soviet casualties. From Moscow, nothing until noon.

choices.text: Cancel the strike and turn to the blockade. Rewrite the speech for a blockade overnight and prepare the proclamation
choices.why: Even at the cost of a few days, go back to a road that can be reversed
choices.after: The pilots were dismissed from the briefing rooms, and LeMay said nothing. The next evening you declared the quarantine on television, and a few of the congressional leaders asked why it had taken so long. The proclamation was signed the day after.

choices.text: Order the strike and the invasion landing together as a single operation. End the missiles and the Castro regime together with an invasion at D+7
choices.why: The military judgment that a war fought halfway is the most dangerous kind
choices.after: With the dawn strike came the announcement of the reserve call-up and the requisition of civilian shipping. The landing ships began to leave the Florida coast. Inside Cuba, some 40,000 Soviet troops moved to the coastal defense lines.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact no air strike was ordered between 16 and 22 October. OPLAN 312 (air strike) and OPLAN 316 (invasion) did exist and appear in General Sweeney's briefing of 21 October and the Joint Chiefs' recommendation of 27 October. The cable recasts those plans in the form of an order. The figure of about 42,000 Soviet troops in Cuba comes from the Soviet-side research report.

JFK-B2.title: Monday Morning
JFK-B2.clock: About 8 hours until OPLAN 312 is executed
JFK-B2.scene: Khrushchev’s letters have gone unanswered or drawn only conditional replies, a U-2 went down on Saturday, and 24 Air Force reserve squadrons have been called up. McNamara says a limited strike is no longer possible: it will take 500 sorties, and invasion is almost inevitable. Low-level photographs show Soviet rocket launchers behind Cuban army positions, and no one can tell whether they have nuclear warheads. There are more than 40,000 Soviet troops in Cuba, and you do not know what orders they have. On Monday morning the pilots take off. Your brother says he can see Dobrynin once more.

voices.text: The photographs show more operational missiles every day. Let Monday pass, and the missiles that survive the strike could be aimed at American cities. If we are going to hit them, it has to be Monday.
Mr. President, Moscow still hasn’t answered what we sent on Saturday night. Give him one more day and he will back down. The letter he wrote on Friday was the work of a frightened man.
I can see Dobrynin once more tonight. Tell him to answer by tomorrow, or we take them out. We can say that and still leave Monday’s order standing.

choices.text: Hold off one more day and send your brother back to Dobrynin, carrying a plain statement that an answer is needed by tomorrow, together with a public letter
choices.why: On the last night, one more knock on the door is the cheaper course
choices.after: You had Monday’s order put back 24 hours. At 7:15 p.m. your brother telephoned Dobrynin. The draft letter was rewritten to answer only yesterday’s letter.

choices.text: Execute OPLAN 312 on Monday morning: 500 sorties, a second-day wave authorized, invasion forces standing by for D+7
choices.why: Every day of waiting adds another operational missile
choices.after: Before dawn on Monday the first wave went in over the island. Soviet surface-to-air missiles fired back, and 12 American planes failed to return on the first day. At noon Radio Moscow announced that orders had been given for a retaliatory strike against the aggression.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. On the night of 27 October the Joint Chiefs recommended an air strike on 29 October and an invasion seven days later, and McNamara later said he had wondered that night whether he would live to see the sun go down the next evening. The United States did not know at the time that there were tactical nuclear warheads in Cuba (12 for the Luna, 80 for the FKR); the figures come from the Soviet Defense Ministry’s withdrawal order of 20 November 1962 (12 Luna warheads, 80 FKR warheads). The Luna (FROG) launchers themselves were identified in low-level photographs on 25 October.

JFK-B3.time: The morning after the air strike
JFK-B3.title: The Second Day
JFK-B3.clock: 2 hours until the second-day wave takes off
JFK-B3.event: Radio Moscow was silent all night, then read a statement in the morning: the Soviet Union will repel aggression against Cuba, and the blood shed by Soviet citizens will be paid for. The Western Allied command in Berlin reports that Soviet troops at the autobahn checkpoints are looking over travel papers longer than usual. The NATO Council has asked for an American explanation, and Macmillan was guarded on the telephone.
JFK-B3.scene: McCone reports. Two-thirds of the known launchers have been destroyed; the rest are under camouflage or never appeared in the photographs. Soviet casualties are estimated in the hundreds. Several American pilots have not come back. Taylor wants to send the second-day wave and bring the invasion landing forward from D+7 to D+3: once the remaining missiles begin preparing to launch, there will be no time. Thompson says now is the moment to write to Khrushchev that the attacks will stop once the missiles are removed. Nitze fears the Soviets will retaliate in Berlin. Moscow has not answered the letter you sent in the night.

voices.text: We should send the second-day wave as planned and bring the landing forward to D+3. We don’t know how many missiles are left, and we cannot give them a week.
Khrushchev hasn’t touched Berlin yet. Send the letter now: the attacks stop once the missiles are removed. We have to give him a sentence he can step back on.

voices.who: Nitze (assistant secretary of defense, Berlin subcommittee)
voices.text: At the autobahn checkpoints the Soviets are taking a long time over the papers. It isn’t a blockade yet. But if they choose Berlin, we will have to fight in two places.

choices.text: Finish the second day’s strikes and stop. Send Khrushchev a letter offering to halt the attacks if the missiles are removed under UN observation
choices.why: Once the missiles are broken, what remains is a deal
choices.after: There was no third day of strikes. Khrushchev’s answer came two days later. It was long and harsh, but it contained a sentence agreeing to remove the remaining missiles under UN observation. Funerals for Soviet personnel were held in Moscow, and the photographs went round the world.

choices.text: Take Taylor’s advice and bring the landing forward: execute OPLAN 316 on D+3 to find and destroy the remaining missiles on the ground
choices.why: A military reckoning: what cannot be seen from the air must be found on the ground
choices.after: The landing ships headed for Cuba’s northwest coast. At dawn on D+3 the spearheads of the Marines and the 1st Armored Division went ashore. Soviet and Cuban resistance was fiercer than expected, and on the second day of the landing the photo interpreters laid new pictures before you.

choices.text: Act on the Berlin reports: reinforce the West Berlin garrison and give the autobahn convoys armed escorts. Halt the Cuban air strikes after the second day
choices.why: Khrushchev’s next move will come in Berlin, not Cuba
choices.after: The next morning Soviet troops at the Helmstedt checkpoint stopped an American convoy. West Berlin had only a few weeks’ supply of electricity and food. The strikes on Cuba stopped, and the two crises overlapped.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. The Special National Intelligence Estimate of 19 October (SNIE 11-18-62) and the Smith memorandum of 23 October judged that Soviet retaliation would fall on American ships elsewhere or on the access routes to Berlin, with Berlin the more likely. The Presidium notes contain no option for a Berlin blockade (per the original).

JFK-B4.title: Retaliatory Strike
JFK-B4.event: After Monday’s strikes, Moscow broadcast that orders had been given for a retaliatory strike against the aggression. The United States does not know what that order means, or what weapons the Soviet commander in Cuba can use. In Berlin, Soviet troops have tightened their checks on the autobahn. In New York U Thant has appealed to both sides for an immediate ceasefire, and Macmillan said on the telephone that if you can stop, you should.
JFK-B4.scene: The second day of strikes is over. Most of the known launchers have been destroyed, but McCone says there may be launchers that never appeared in the photographs. More than 20 American aircraft have been lost, and Soviet and Cuban casualties are estimated in the thousands. Taylor wants to go ahead with the D+7 landing, and McNamara brings out photographs showing Soviet rocket units behind the landing beaches. No one knows whether those rockets carry nuclear warheads. Thompson says Khrushchev has still not touched Berlin, so now is the time to stop and send a letter. Khrushchev’s Friday letter still lies on your desk, unanswered.

voices.text: We’ve knocked out nearly all the known launchers. But they may have moved some at night, and there may be some that never showed up in the photographs. Short of going in on the ground, there is no way to be sure.

There are Soviet rocket units behind the landing beaches, field rockets with a range of about 30 kilometers. We don’t know what warheads they carry. If we land, those rockets will come down on the beaches.
He still hasn’t touched Berlin. That means he wants to end this. Stop now and send the letter: remove them, and there will be no invasion.

choices.text: Go ahead with the landing: execute OPLAN 316 on D+7, find and destroy the remaining missiles on the ground, and disarm the Soviet forces
choices.why: A military reckoning: what cannot be seen from the air must be found on the ground
choices.after: At dawn on D+7 the spearheads of the Marines and the 1st Armored Division went ashore on Cuba’s northwest coast. Resistance was fierce. On the second day of the landing the photo interpreters laid new pictures before you.

choices.text: Stop with the air strikes. Answer Khrushchev’s Friday letter, offering to halt the attacks and pledge no invasion if the remaining missiles are removed under UN observation
choices.why: What has been destroyed is enough; what remains is a deal
choices.after: There was no third day of strikes. Khrushchev’s answer came two days later. It was long and harsh, but it contained a sentence agreeing to remove the remaining missiles under UN observation. Funerals for Soviet personnel were held in Moscow, and the photographs went round the world.

choices.text: Act on the Berlin reports: reinforce the West Berlin garrison and give the convoys armed escorts. Put the Cuban landing on hold
choices.why: Khrushchev’s next move will come in Berlin, not Cuba
choices.after: The next morning Soviet troops at the Helmstedt checkpoint stopped an American convoy. The Cuban landing was halted, and the two crises overlapped.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Khrushchev’s statement at the Presidium on 28 October that “we gave the order to deliver a retaliatory strike if an attack is provoked” is found in a Soviet-side research report (Protocol No. 63). The Soviet Luna (FROG) launchers in Cuba were identified in low-level photographs on 25 October, but the United States did not learn of their 12 nuclear warheads until 1992.

JFK-G1.time: Morning of the second day ashore
JFK-G1.title: Luna
JFK-G1.clock: No telling how long the landing force can hold the beachhead
JFK-G1.event: On the first night ashore, flashes lit the sky over two assembly areas behind the beachhead. Casualties run into the thousands, and one sector of the beachhead no longer exists. A Luna, a Soviet field rocket, has been fired with a nuclear warhead. No one knows whether Moscow ordered it or a commander on the spot decided. Radio Moscow is silent.
JFK-G1.scene: For the first time McNamara’s voice shakes. It was a tactical nuclear weapon, Mr. President. Taylor says the answer must be the same weapon against the Soviet assembly areas in Cuba, or the rest of the landing force will be wiped out. LeMay says to look not at Cuba but at the bases on Soviet soil. Rusk says Moscow’s silence may mean they did not know either, and Thompson says that if the United States answers with nuclear weapons now, the next flash will be over Berlin or Turkey. Your brother watches your face. Two orders lie before you: one for tactical nuclear retaliation, the other for withdrawing the landing force and offering a ceasefire.

voices.text: Unless we answer the two assembly areas with the same weapon, the troops on the beachhead won’t last the night. Tactical nuclear retaliation, confined to Cuba. Soviet soil is not touched.

There is no such thing as a nuclear exchange confined to Cuba. If we answer with nuclear weapons, Khrushchev cannot avoid answering in front of the Presidium, and his answer will fall on Turkey or Berlin. These few hours of silence from Moscow are the last chance.

We can get the landing force out today. The losses are heavy, but there is no point in holding the beachhead. The air strikes have already destroyed most of the missile sites. We can offer a ceasefire and pull out.

choices.text: Do not answer with nuclear weapons. Take the landing force off by sea, continue only conventional bombing, and offer Khrushchev an immediate ceasefire and removal under UN observation
choices.why: If the first nuclear weapon is to be the last, the second must never be used
choices.after: The Marines went back to their ships that night. Khrushchev’s answer came 12 hours later. It explained that a commander on the spot had acted on his own, and it promised to withdraw all nuclear weapons under UN observation. The world had to take that explanation on trust.

choices.text: Answer with tactical nuclear weapons against the Soviet assembly areas in Cuba. Confine it to Cuba and leave Soviet soil untouched
choices.why: Leave this unanswered, and in the next war everyone will use nuclear weapons first
choices.after: At noon flashes rose over two assembly areas in central Cuba. Moscow’s silence lasted six more hours. What happened next you will see in the Ending.

choices.text: Hold the beachhead but use no nuclear weapons. Notify Khrushchev that unless all nuclear weapons are withdrawn within 24 hours, you will move to the next step
choices.why: The resolve not to back down, and not to cross the last line either
choices.after: The beachhead held that night, at a heavy price. Khrushchev’s answer came 20 hours later, saying the commander on the spot had been relieved and promising to withdraw the nuclear weapons under UN observation. American troops held a stretch of coast in northwestern Cuba for months while the negotiations went on.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Whether authority to use tactical nuclear weapons had been delegated in advance to the Soviet forces in Cuba is disputed (the instruction of 8 September was an unsigned draft, Order No. 4/389 of 22 October excluded nuclear weapons, and No. 76639 of 27 October repeated the prohibition), and most scholars hold that no valid delegation existed on paper. The damage estimates for the nuclear-exchange endings were meant to quote American government documents of the time, but this lay outside the scope of the Phase 1 research.

JFK-C1.place: Situation Room → Cabinet Room, the White House
JFK-C1.title: An Eye for an Eye
JFK-C1.clock: No telling when Moscow will answer
JFK-C1.event: At dawn tactical aircraft struck the SAM site at Banes in eastern Cuba. The site was destroyed and dozens of Soviet personnel were killed. Other SAM sites fired on the escort aircraft, and two American planes went down. At 9 a.m. Radio Moscow read not yesterday’s Khrushchev letter but a Soviet government statement: Soviet forces in Cuba have orders to deliver a retaliatory strike if aggression begins. Last night’s violation of Soviet airspace by the U-2 from Alaska is included in the statement.
JFK-C1.scene: McNamara says that since every SAM site will now fire on American planes, reconnaissance is impossible without air strikes. Taylor wants to go ahead with OPLAN 312 on Monday. Thompson notes that the statement says nothing about removing the missiles: they have not shut the door yet. Your brother says the cable Dobrynin sent to Moscow last night will have arrived before this morning’s statement. Rusk worries that the Soviets may read the Alaska U-2 as reconnaissance before an attack. SAC is on full alert, and the Soviets will be too. The public letter you wrote yesterday evening is still on your desk. Either you did not send it, or, if you did, this morning’s strike has blurred its meaning.

voices.text: Now that the SAM sites have fired back, we can’t fly reconnaissance without strikes. Monday’s 312 has to go ahead. If we stop, they’ll read it as America hitting once and backing off.

The statement says nothing about removing the missiles. They haven’t withdrawn yesterday’s letter. Send the letter now: this morning was the answer to yesterday’s shootdown, and there will be no more.
The Alaska U-2 is in the statement. They may read it as reconnaissance before an attack. If we strike on Monday, that reading will look right.

choices.text: Stop here. Send a public letter answering only yesterday’s letter, state that the morning strike was solely a reply to the shootdown, and send your brother
choices.why: After striking once, you must open the door again if the other side is to come through it
choices.after: At noon the letter left for Moscow, and your brother met Dobrynin and told him to answer by tomorrow. Moscow’s answer came by radio the next morning: dismantle, crate, return. It came a day later than in history, and in between, Moscow buried dozens of Soviet personnel.

choices.text: Go ahead with OPLAN 312 on Monday. Now that the SAM sites have fired back, the missile sites and the SAMs must be hit together before reconnaissance is possible
choices.why: Military judgment: an attack once begun means something only if it is carried through
choices.after: Before dawn on Monday the first wave went in over the island. Soviet surface-to-air missiles fired back, and 12 American planes failed to return on the first day. Radio Moscow repeated the retaliatory strike order.

choices.text: Clear the skies first: hit every SAM site and airfield in Cuba this afternoon. Decide on the missile sites after tomorrow’s reconnaissance
choices.why: Protect the reconnaissance planes first; after that, the photographs will tell you what to do
choices.after: In the afternoon 24 SAM sites and the airfields were struck. That night the photographs showed work on the missile sites going on around the clock, and the next morning you ordered strikes on the missile sites.

In fact on 23 October the Executive Committee agreed that if a U-2 was shot down, the most likely SAM site would be hit in immediate retaliation, but on the evening of 27 October the President put that retaliation off by a day. JFK-D0.title: The Turkish Card
JFK-D0.clock: About 38 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (10 a.m. on the 24th)

map.caption: The 15 Jupiters at Çiğli air base near Izmir were fully deployed by the spring of 1962. With a range of about 2,400 kilometers, they were aimed at the southern Soviet Union.

JFK-D0.event: Word reached Moscow that the United States had linked Turkey with Cuba. Khrushchev seized on it as if he had been waiting for it. In its evening broadcast Radio Moscow announced to the world a proposal that the Soviet Union remove weapons of this kind from Cuba and the United States remove the same kind from Turkey. Ambassador Hare in Ankara sent an urgent cable, and Finletter in Paris reported that the NATO Council was in uproar. General Norstad wrote urging that the exchange be refused.
JFK-D0.scene: Bundy left the room and came back. We must not be seen to sell out an ally, he keeps repeating. Rusk says Turkey should have been told first, and McNamara says that militarily the Jupiters make no difference at all: one Polaris submarine can stand in for all 15. Your brother says that now Moscow is demanding it in public, there can be no secret deal; only a public trade or a refusal is left. Macmillan said slowly on the telephone that a deal behind an ally’s back could turn into a Munich. The card you played is on the table, and taking it back has a price too.

voices.text: We can’t settle Cuba while looking as if we’re selling out an ally. Turkey is a country we have pledged to defend. Take the card back. Taking it back costs less than playing it.
Militarily we can do without the Jupiters. One Polaris submarine stands in for all 15, and it is safer. The problem is how the Turkish government and NATO read it, not the missiles.

Now that they’re asking for it in public, the secret deal is gone. Either we accept it in public, or we refuse it in public and go to the blockade. That’s all. And Jack, if we refuse, you’ll have taken back the card you played yourself.

choices.text: Take the card back. Declare publicly that Turkey is not up for trade, and go ahead with the blockade speech and proclamation. Assure NATO of American resolve
choices.why: Taking back a card already played costs less than playing it
choices.after: The statement went out, and the Turkish foreign minister publicly regretted that the United States had brought up Turkey at all. Moscow mocked the American reversal. That night you spoke to Macmillan, and the road to the blockade was narrower than it had been at the start.

choices.text: Accept the public exchange. Remove the 15 Jupiters in Turkey and the missiles in Cuba at the same time under UN observation, and promise Turkey a Polaris deployment
choices.why: If 15 useless missiles can end the crisis, that is the cheapest price there is
choices.after: Khrushchev accepted within hours. There were demonstrations in Ankara, and the NATO Council in Paris asked for an American explanation. The missiles already in Cuba were still where they were, and verification was only beginning.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact, on 18 October the President raised the withdrawal of the missiles in Turkey as a question (McCone’s record); on 20 October Stevenson proposed a Turkey–Guantánamo exchange; and the 11 a.m. meeting on 22 October considered a plan to withdraw all nuclear weapons from non-nuclear countries at once. None of these was adopted. On 23 October Ormsby-Gore reported to London that the President had no military objection to a mutual closing of bases, and wrote that this was not to be revealed to any American.

JFK-D1.title: The Public Deal
JFK-D1.clock: A few hours until the emergency meeting of the NATO Council (Paris)
JFK-D1.event: Radio Moscow welcomed the American answer and announced that the missiles in Cuba had been ordered removed. The Turkish foreign minister stated publicly that his government had not been consulted in advance about the American decision, and there were demonstrations in Ankara and Istanbul. General Norstad sent a cable hinting at resignation, and Adenauer asked whether West Berlin was next. Macmillan said on the telephone that a deal behind an ally’s back could turn into a Munich. In Havana, Castro raged that Cuba had been made a bargaining chip.
JFK-D1.scene: McNamara has come with a report that a single Polaris submarine in the Mediterranean is a better deterrent than the 15 Jupiters. Rusk says the problem is how to put that to Turkey. Bundy says NATO will now go back over every American commitment. Your brother says getting the missiles out of Cuba comes first; NATO can be soothed afterward. Khrushchev has said he will have the Turkish removal verified by UN observation, and the United States will have the Cuban removal verified the same way. What remains is how to match the two removals. The crisis is ending fast, and the price is being paid in Europe.

voices.text: One Polaris submarine is better than 15 Jupiters. We just have to show Turkey that. Deterrence has gone up, and Turkey is safer. The problem isn’t numbers, it’s face.

NATO will now go back over every commitment we have made: Berlin, West Germany, Norway. What they are asking is not about the Jupiters. It’s what else America will give up the next time the Soviets lean on it.
The Cuban missiles have to go first. We soothe NATO after that. Let Khrushchev move first, and have the Turkish removal start only after the UN observers are in Cuba.

choices.text: Match the two removals by sequence: begin the Turkish removal only once the Cuban removal has been confirmed under UN observation, and promise Turkey a Polaris deployment
choices.why: Even after a deal, the order of steps can save part of the face
choices.after: Khrushchev accepted the sequence. In November the missiles in Cuba were loaded onto ships, and early in 1963 the Jupiters at Izmir were dismantled. The NATO Council heard the American explanation, but for years afterward Europe kept going back over America’s commitments.

choices.text: Accept simultaneous removal: UN observers enter Cuba and Turkey on the same day, and Turkey is compensated with Polaris afterward
choices.why: A quick settlement is worth more than the ally’s face
choices.after: UN observers entered Havana and Izmir together in the first week of November. The crisis was over within two weeks. The Turkish parliament argued fiercely over staying in NATO, and from that winter on de Gaulle said more and more often that Europe must defend itself.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact, after McNamara proposed replacing them with Polaris at the NATO ministerial meeting in December 1962, the last of the Jupiters in Turkey was dismantled on 24 April 1963, and on 29 October the Turkish government thanked the United States for refusing any deal. The record shows that when the Vice President asked on the evening of 27 October why not make the trade, Ball spoke of replacing the Jupiters with Polaris.

JFK-E1.title: The Freeze
JFK-E1.clock: About two weeks until the freeze runs out
JFK-E1.event: Both sides have accepted U Thant’s freeze proposal. The United States has stopped intercepting ships at the quarantine line and the Soviet Union has stopped its shipments, while in New York Stevenson and Zorin negotiate in the acting secretary-general’s office. Whether work on the missile sites in Cuba has stopped can be known only from photographs, and every morning McCone reports that it is continuing. The Soviets have demanded that reconnaissance flights stop too while the freeze lasts.
JFK-E1.scene: It is the third day of talks. Zorin keeps repeating that the weapons in Cuba are defensive, and the Soviet delegation brings up a no-invasion guarantee, Guantánamo and Turkey by turns. Stevenson says a framework can be built within two weeks. McCone lays down his photographs: at Sagua la Grande work goes on every night despite the freeze, and the number of operational launchers grows by one a day. Taylor says the freeze gives the Soviets time, and when it runs out, an air strike will cost twice as much. Congressional leaders complain that America is being dragged along by the UN on the eve of the election, and Macmillan says on the telephone that he supports the UN route but there must be verification.

voices.who: Stevenson (ambassador to the UN, from New York)
voices.text: We can build a framework within two weeks: a no-invasion guarantee, removal under UN observation, and the neutralization of Cuba. Zorin is waiting for instructions, and Moscow wants to end this.
The freeze exists only on paper. At Sagua la Grande the work goes on every night. We get one more operational launcher a day. In two weeks they will all be operational.
Strike when the freeze ends and the losses will double. Every SAM will be working and every missile standing. If you mean to strike, strike now. If not, you must be ready never to strike at all.

choices.text: Keep negotiating. Even if the work goes on, spend the two weeks winning terms that let UN observers in
choices.why: A path begun with words must be finished with words
choices.after: The talks ran past two weeks. In the 6 November elections the President’s party held the Senate but lost seats in the House, and the newspapers named Cuba as the reason. U Thant went to Havana, and Castro refused the observers.

choices.text: Release the photographs showing work going on during the freeze, and declare the talks broken off. Have Monday’s air strike readied
choices.why: Make the side that broke the freeze bear the blame, and the strike has its justification
choices.after: The photographs ran on the front pages. In New York Stevenson spoke of resigning, and U Thant appealed to both sides again. Taylor briefed you on OPLAN 312 for Monday morning.

choices.text: Put the Turkish exchange on the table publicly during the freeze and close the talks. Have the UN observe both removals together
choices.why: If missiles keep going up while the talks drag on, it is better to finish quickly
choices.after: Zorin had his instructions within a day. Ankara protested publicly, and the NATO Council in Paris was called into emergency session.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. U Thant’s first appeal on 24 October proposed a voluntary suspension of two to three weeks; on 26 October Stevenson negotiated a 24–48-hour freeze proposal, but McCone opposed it and it was not adopted. Ormsby-Gore’s memorandum of 24 October recorded that Macmillan had seen the earlier freeze proposal, but that he himself was against it.

JFK-E2.title: Third Week of the Freeze
JFK-E2.clock: Five days until the General Assembly debate on Cuba
JFK-E2.event: In Havana U Thant asked Castro to accept observers and was refused. The Cuban government said an American pledge not to invade must come first, and the return of Guantánamo was a condition. In New York the Soviet representative Kuznetsov said the missiles were under Soviet control and that no observers could be admitted without the Cuban government’s consent. McCone has reported that every launcher is now operational. The election is over, and the Republicans are attacking you over Cuba.
JFK-E2.scene: The quarantine survives in name only; the Soviet ships lie stopped where they are. Stevenson says he can get a General Assembly resolution out of this, a non-invasion pledge and a phased withdrawal. McNamara says that with every missile now operational, an air strike could bring on a preemptive nuclear attack. Bundy says quietly that there is another way: accept the missiles in Cuba as America accepts Soviet intercontinental missiles, lift the quarantine and prepare for the next crisis. No one welcomes the thought, and no one can refute it. The reports from Berlin are quiet.

voices.text: We can get a resolution through the Assembly. A non-invasion pledge, a phased withdrawal, and a nuclear-free zone in the Caribbean. It takes time, but there is a way.

The United States lives with Soviet intercontinental missiles. Someone has to say that we can live with the missiles in Cuba the same way. Lift the quarantine, and prepare for the next crisis. The price will be paid in Berlin.
The missiles are all operational. An air strike can now bring on a first launch from their side. The options we had on October 16 no longer exist.

choices.text: Follow the UN route to the end. Build a framework of non-invasion pledge and phased withdrawal through a General Assembly resolution, and keep the quarantine until that framework stands
choices.why: An ending the UN builds, however slow, will last longest
choices.after: The Assembly resolution passed in December, and the missiles came out in stages through the spring of 1963. All the while American aircraft flew over Cuba every day, and Castro never admitted the observers.

choices.text: Lift the quarantine and acquiesce in the missiles. Treat them like Soviet intercontinental missiles, and prepare for the next crisis without an air strike
choices.why: Striking missiles that are all operational is choosing war
choices.after: The quarantine was lifted on November 20. The announcement did not use the word missiles. In the spring, Khrushchev raised the Berlin question again.

choices.text: Declare the negotiations broken off and strike. Even with every missile operational, this is better than leaving them in place
choices.why: A late strike is still better than acquiescence
choices.after: In the small hours of a day in the third week of November, the air strike began. The Soviets answered in Berlin, and the Soviet forces in Cuba, facing no landing, did not use the weapons they could have used. What followed, you will see in the ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In reality, in November the withdrawal was verified not by UN observers but by Red Cross inspection at sea and by American low-level photography, and Castro refused the observers. The results of the midterm election of November 6, 1962 (Democrats up four seats in the Senate, 64 to 68, and down three in the House, 262 to 259) are the real figures. The logic of “accepting them like Soviet intercontinental missiles” has its roots in McNamara’s remarks on the evening of October 16.

JFK-F1.title: Waiting
JFK-F1.clock: A few hours until the election returns
JFK-F1.event: The United States never answered the public proposal of October 27 in public. Private letters went back and forth and the blockade was kept in place. The Soviet ships have lain stopped outside the quarantine line for three weeks, while construction in Cuba went on until every launcher was operational. Khrushchev has said publicly that since the United States did not answer the Turkey proposal, the weapons in Cuba will stay where they are. The General Assembly has opened its debate on Cuba, and Congress is demanding an air strike even on election day.
JFK-F1.scene: McCone says every missile is operational and he still does not know whether there are nuclear warheads. McNamara says an air strike could now bring on a preemptive nuclear attack. Bundy speaks of living with the missiles in Cuba as America lives with Soviet intercontinental missiles, and adds that the price would be paid in Berlin. Nitze comes in. Soviet troops have stopped an American convoy at a checkpoint on the Berlin autobahn. It is not yet a closure. Your brother asks you: is the waiting over, or not yet?

voices.text: The United States lives with Soviet intercontinental missiles over its head. We can live with the missiles in Cuba the same way. If you are willing to be the president who says so, the price will be paid in Europe.
They are all operational. An air strike can now bring on a first launch from their side. The options we had on October 16 no longer exist. There is nothing to do but hold the blockade.

Soviet troops have stopped an American convoy at the Helmstedt checkpoint. They call it a document check. It is not a closure yet. But if they choose Berlin, the blockade of Cuba and a blockade of Berlin will overlap.

choices.text: Acquiesce while keeping the blockade. Say nothing more about the missiles, neither strike nor trade, and prepare for the next crisis
choices.why: Unspoken acquiescence is cheaper than public defeat
choices.after: The quarantine was quietly lifted at the end of November. The missiles stayed where they were, and in the spring Khrushchev raised the Berlin question again.

choices.text: Act on the Berlin report: reinforce the West Berlin garrison and give the convoys armed escorts. Leave Cuba under blockade
choices.why: Khrushchev’s next move is Berlin, and there is no backing down there
choices.after: The next morning, Soviet troops at Helmstedt barred the convoy’s passage. The two blockades now overlapped.

choices.text: Strike, even now. Better to hit missiles that are all operational than to acquiesce in them
choices.why: A late strike is still better than acquiescence
choices.after: In the small hours of a day in the second week of November, the air strike began. The Soviets answered in Berlin, and the Soviet forces in Cuba, facing no landing, did not use the weapons they could have used. What followed, you will see in the ending.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. On October 27 Ball proposed not answering the public letter in public and sending only a private letter, and the Serov memorandum for the Presidium of October 25 contained the idea of withdrawing only the R-12s and leaving the rest (according to the Soviet-side research report). There is no record of the U.S. government formally considering a plan that accepted the missiles staying in Cuba; McNamara’s remarks of October 16 are the root of that logic.

JFK-H1.title: Helmstedt
JFK-H1.clock: West Berlin stockpiles: food for more than six months, coal for about a year
JFK-H1.event: Soviet troops at the Helmstedt checkpoint have barred an American convoy from passing. The railway to West Berlin has also been halted, on the pretext of document checks. Moscow has announced that it will control the access routes to Berlin until the American blockade of Cuba is lifted. What is different from 1948 is that this time both sides have nuclear weapons. Adenauer asked on the telephone whether the United States would trade Berlin for Cuba, and Macmillan spoke of a conference to settle both crises at once.
JFK-H1.scene: General Norstad reports a plan to force the autobahn with an armed convoy. If the Soviets block it, the first shots will be fired in the middle of Europe. McNamara says an airlift is possible, as in 1948, but it will be a different matter if Soviet fighters interfere. Thompson says Khrushchev chose Berlin because he is looking for a way out of Cuba: his aim is to trade the lifting of the Cuban blockade for the reopening of access to Berlin. Bundy says this is exactly what Macmillan wrote on October 22 must be avoided at any price. Two roads lie before you: push the convoy through, or put both blockades on one table.

voices.who: Norstad (Supreme Allied Commander Europe, from Paris)
voices.text: We can force Helmstedt with an armed convoy. If the Soviets block it, the first shots will be fired. But if we do not force it, West Berlin will be squeezed within months.
He chose Berlin because he is looking for a way out of Cuba. Lift the Cuban blockade and he will open Berlin. Accept that trade, and next he will put Berlin itself on the table.

It is exactly what Macmillan wrote on October 22: that Khrushchev would try to trade his position in Cuba for his ambitions in Berlin, and that this must be avoided at any price. Now you have to set that price.

choices.text: Force the autobahn with an armed convoy. Keep the Cuban blockade as it is, and declare that access to Berlin is not a subject for negotiation
choices.why: Only by standing firm in both places can either be held
choices.after: The convoy halted in front of Soviet tanks, and the two sides faced each other for three days without firing. Through those three days both blockades held, and the world watched two maps at once.

choices.text: Put both blockades on one table. Propose a conference that takes up the withdrawal of the Cuban missiles and the restoration of access to Berlin together
choices.why: Settle both crises as one, and neither side has to back down alone anywhere
choices.after: The conference met in Geneva in December. Berlin was opened and the missiles left Cuba in stages by spring, but West Germany did not forget that the United States had put Berlin on the negotiating table.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. There is no plan for a blockade of Berlin in the Soviet Presidium memoranda (original text). The Western fears appear in McNamara’s remarks of October 16, Macmillan’s cable of October 22, the CIA Smith memorandum of October 23 (retaliation more likely on the Berlin access routes), and the British Strong report of November 1962 (American thinking in case of a Berlin counterstroke). The West Berlin stockpile figures are the estimates in the CIA Office of National Estimates memorandum of October 23, 1962 (food for more than six months, coal for about a year, medicines for six months).

JFK-S1.title: First Shot on the High Seas
JFK-S1.clock: About ten hours until the Security Council reconvenes (4 p.m.)
JFK-S1.event: A destroyer signaled a Soviet ship to heave to, and the ship did not stop. It did not stop after warning shots either. The Navy is asking for permission to fire into the propellers. There may be a submarine beneath the Soviet ship, and Moscow said in yesterday’s letter that it had instructed its captains not to obey the orders of the U.S. Navy. In New York, Zorin is demanding that the Security Council reconvene and preparing to use the word piracy.
JFK-S1.scene: Admiral Anderson, the chief of naval operations, says that if they fire into the propellers the ship will stop, and if it does not, a boarding party will go aboard. McNamara says that tanker or passenger ship, the vessel flies the Soviet flag, and if Soviet crewmen die Khrushchev will have to answer. Thompson says the answer will come not at sea but in Berlin. Your brother repeats that striking the missiles in Cuba is better than stopping Soviet ships on the high seas. Dillon says the confrontation should take place in Cuba. You have minutes to decide. Out on the water, a captain is waiting for orders.

voices.text: I request permission to fire into the propellers. If we fire, the ship stops. If it does not, a boarding party goes aboard. The captain is waiting for orders.
If Soviet crewmen die, Khrushchev will have to answer before the Presidium. That answer will not come at sea. It will come on the Berlin autobahn.
The confrontation should be in Cuba, not on the high seas. Firing on a Soviet ship at sea points the gun more directly at the Soviet Union than striking the missiles does.

choices.text: Authorize firing into the propellers and forcible boarding. The blockade has to be enforced once for all to see, and this is the first ship
choices.why: A line declared and not held is a line never declared
choices.after: The destroyer fired into the propellers and the ship stopped. Three crewmen were killed. Moscow called it piracy, and two days later Soviet troops at the Helmstedt checkpoint barred an American convoy.

choices.text: Stop at the warning shots and let the ship through. Return to the U Thant route instead of a confrontation at sea, and reset the rules to apply from the next ship on
choices.why: Where the first shot is fired decides the shape of the war
choices.after: The ship sailed into Havana, and Havana celebrated. The congressional leadership said the blockade had been breached. Stevenson met U Thant again in New York, and the next day Khrushchev’s long letter came in.

choices.text: Authorize sinking the ship if it resists. Since the Soviets have ordered their captains not to comply, break that order at sea
choices.why: Only by nullifying the other side’s order at sea will the next ship stop
choices.after: The ship did not stop even after the shots into the propellers, and the destroyer’s next salvo left the hull listing. Most of the crew were rescued, but not all. Two days later Soviet troops at Helmstedt barred an American convoy.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In reality, no Soviet-flag ship was fired on during the quarantine, and the only boarding and search was of the Lebanese-registered Marucla on October 26. The CIA Smith memorandum of October 23 judged that if the Soviets tested the blockade, they would more likely refuse boarding with a non-military freighter, exploit an American attack, and then retaliate on the Berlin access routes.

epilogues.A: On 20 November you announced the lifting of the quarantine, and the Il-28 bombers were loaded onto ships in December. The last of the Jupiters in Turkey was dismantled on 24 April 1963, and that spring Polaris submarines entered the Mediterranean. In June a hot line was laid between Washington and Moscow, and in August the Partial Test Ban Treaty was signed. What your brother said to Dobrynin on the night of 27 October was not officially acknowledged by the United States government until the 1980s. At that same hour, at the dacha at Novo-Ogaryovo, the Presidium was waiting for Dobrynin’s cable.
epilogues.B: The air strike destroyed most of the known missiles, and several hundred Soviet personnel died. Khrushchev agreed to remove the remaining missiles under UN supervision, but the funeral photographs from Moscow and the anti-American demonstrations across Latin America were the price American diplomacy paid for years afterward. Had the Monday strike the Joint Chiefs recommended been put off by a single day, no one knows whether Moscow would have answered within that day.
epilogues.C: The decisions taken in the hours after the second flash over Cuba shaped the world that followed. Washington learned from that flash that there had been tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba. The scale of the damage survives in the estimates the United States government drew up at the time.
epilogues.D: The missiles left Cuba in November, and the Jupiters left Turkey that winter. The crisis was over in two weeks, but for years afterward NATO counted America’s promises over again, and de Gaulle said more often that Europe must be defended by Europeans. On 27 October you had said it would look like a very fair trade; that was the road you took, and you took it in public.
epilogues.E: Under a General Assembly resolution and U Thant’s mediation, the missiles left in stages through the spring of 1963. Castro never admitted the observers, and until that spring the United States flew over Cuba every day. While a freeze of two or three weeks stretched into a season, McCone brought photographs to every meeting showing that construction was going on.
epilogues.F: The missiles stayed where they were, and the United States began to live with missiles in Cuba as it lived with Soviet intercontinental missiles. In the spring of 1963 Khrushchev raised the Berlin question again, and with the defeat in that year’s midterm elections, Cuba became the first issue of the next presidential campaign.
epilogues.G: A tactical nuclear weapon was used on Cuba’s northwest coast, and the United States did not answer with nuclear weapons. The landing force lost thousands of men. Moscow explained it as the unauthorized act of a local commander and withdrew all its nuclear weapons under UN supervision. The world had to believe that explanation, and nuclear weapons were never used on a battlefield again. Whether that commander had the authority was never established.
epilogues.H: The tanks at Helmstedt pulled back three days later, and the Geneva conference took up Berlin access and the removal of the Cuban missiles together. West Germany did not forget that the United States had put Berlin on the negotiating table, and the Europe of 1963 was not the Europe of 1962.
