dossier.t: Born in Brookline, Massachusetts, on 29 May 1917, he is 45 in October 1962. In November 1960 he beat Nixon by a narrow margin to become the youngest man ever elected president, and he has now been in office a year and nine months. As a congressman and senator he was called a politician raised on his father’s money and connections, and he made his name in the war when he lost his torpedo boat, PT-109, in the Pacific and saved his crew. Diagnosed with Addison’s disease in 1947, he took cortisone-type drugs for the rest of his life, and after spinal operations in 1954 and 1955 his back pain persisted, treated with painkillers and injections together. This medical history was denied during the campaign and was never disclosed after he became president. He speaks briefly and quickly, and when briefed he has a habit of asking back about the numbers and the odds. At the afternoon meeting of 16 October he said he still could not understand why the Soviets had put missiles in Cuba, and that there had been no provocation as clear-cut since the Berlin blockade. In the Cabinet Room and the Oval Office a tape recorder you had secretly installed is running, and your advisers do not know they are being recorded.

His brother Robert is the 36-year-old attorney general and the only person in the White House who can speak to you without ceremony. On 16 October he said the fifth alternative was invasion; on the 19th he invoked the memory of Pearl Harbor against a strike without warning; and on the 21st he said again that a Monday strike would be a Pearl Harbor–style attack. Their father, Joseph, has barely been able to speak since a stroke in December 1961. Bundy, the national security adviser, took Deputy Director Carter’s call on the night of the 15th and did not wake you; he later wrote that it had been a hell of a secret. McNamara, the secretary of defense, said this was a domestic political problem, not a military one; Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, wanted to strike without warning; and LeMay, the Air Force chief of staff, compared a blockade to the appeasement at Munich. Rusk, the secretary of state; Thompson, the Soviet expert; Sorensen, who writes the speeches; Dillon, the secretary of the treasury; and Stevenson, the ambassador to the UN, gathered in the same room every day, and former secretary of state Acheson said to stop talking and act at once. The British ambassador, Ormsby-Gore, is an old friend; at lunch on the 21st he became the first person outside the United States government to be told, and he and Macmillan spoke by telephone night after night.

The failure at the Bay of Pigs in April 1961 is a memory that has not yet closed. On 16 October Taylor said there was a war plan to send 250,000 Americans against the island where 1,800 Cubans had been sent a year and a half earlier, and you have admitted to Gromyko and to Khrushchev alike that the landing was a mistake. After the Vienna summit in June came the verdict that Khrushchev had pushed you around, and in August the Wall went up in Berlin. Because you said in public on 4 September and 13 September that the gravest issues would arise if offensive weapons came in, to see the missiles and do nothing would make those words empty. The midterm elections of 6 November are three weeks away, and Senator Keating keeps saying there are offensive weapons in Cuba. Domestic politics narrows your choices to the point where people say that to back down would mean impeachment. The greatest fear is nuclear war, which at the meeting on the 18th you called the final failure. The hope is that Khrushchev is a rational man, and that if he is given a way out that does not look like total surrender, he can step back.

movers.intro: Why Kennedy chose a blockade over an air strike, and why on the last night he privately promised the Turkish missiles, are questions still argued over even after the tape transcripts and the Soviet documents were released. Another point of dispute is that the picture painted in Robert Kennedy’s memoir, Thirteen Days, differs from the one on the tapes. The main views are these:
views: Graham Allison and Philip Zelikow: hold that the blockade decision cannot be explained as one man’s rational choice alone. They point out that the Air Force would guarantee destroying only up to 90 percent of the known missiles, that the Navy ran the blockade by its own procedures, and that bargaining among the advisers changed the outcome, and argue that organizations and politics inside the government had narrowed the President’s options in advance.

Aleksandr Fursenko and Timothy Naftali: read the Soviet documents as showing that Khrushchev was already leaning toward withdrawal by 25 October, and hold that whether the decision of the 28th came before he saw Dobrynin’s cable is open to both readings. They see Kennedy as far more open to a deal than his advisers, and willing to accept the Turkish trade even in public.

Michael Dobbs: shows that the dramatic moment of 24 October, when Soviet ships turned back before the blockade line, was in fact the result of a recall order Moscow had issued the day before. Citing the Alaskan U-2’s stray into Soviet airspace and the B-59 submarine incident, he holds that chance and luck did more to decide how the crisis ended than the control of the two leaders.

Sheldon Stern: holds that anyone who reads the tape transcripts whole finds that the most moderate man in the room was the President himself, and that Robert Kennedy’s memoir inflated his own role and concealed how close his brother came to the Turkish trade. At the same time he points out that Operation Mongoose and the Bay of Pigs produced Khrushchev’s decision to deploy, so that Kennedy too bears responsibility for the crisis.
movers.note: Some have argued that Kennedy’s illness and medication affected his judgment during the crisis, but there is a strong counterargument that the tapes and minutes of the thirteen days show no trace of it. The Cordier channel that Rusk disclosed in 1987 is the main evidence for the reading that Kennedy was prepared to go as far as a public trade.
